madam president, i would like to draw attention to an unacceptable situation for romania, which is treated as a second-rate country. in 2007, we joined the european union in recognition of the efforts and progress made in almost every field. however, entry into the schengen area was postponed in order to meet special technical security conditions. today, romania's borders meet all the technical conditions assumed, which is recognized by all those responsible for the area, while being a provider of security and stability, both for the region and for the entire union. however, we are being unjustifiably denied access to the schengen area on pretexts that are unacceptable for a europe that wants to be respectable. this creates unfair competition between romanian and foreign companies, seriously affecting the movement of goods and the lives of romanian citizens. therefore, we must say it loud and clear: romania must be treated equally with the other member states of the european union, it must enjoy all the full rights, and joining the schengen area is not only a right of romania, but also an obligation of the european union!

in writing. i am in favour of unlocking the european decision-making process on the authorisation of gmos at european level. the legislative proposal is intended to respond to the request of the member states of the european union to be able to restrict or prohibit, as appropriate, the cultivation of a gmo crop and does not change the european authorisation system. the fact that member states that will grow gmos will be obliged to take measures to avoid cross-border contamination must also be considered as respecting the decision of other states that decide differently. the positive or negative effects of a gmo crop remain for the assessment of scientific operators. in romania, universities and research institutions need to become more involved in this area, to collaborate more with their european counterparts and to carefully analyse the studies carried out by efsa, in order to provide the necessary decision-making basis for the policy actors. in this context, i am convinced that only thorough research can provide adequate protection of the environment and the health of european citizens. we need more public debate by scientific researchers together with academia, the op, civil society and government institutions to clarify the effects of gmo crops.
in writing. i welcome this regulation which confirms the right of member states to prohibit the cultivation of genetically modified organisms on their territory. many european citizens are concerned about the as yet unknown environmental effects of gmos. but until now, member states that wanted to ban these crops faced legislative uncertainty and feared legal sanctions. this regulation will change the situation, because it provides a basis for the ban of gmos at the level of each state. in addition, it will also ensure improved safety assessments for gmos, including mandatory buffer zones to prevent contamination of crops in border regions. these are really important and positive steps. but there is also a significant risk that we must take into account. the commission has also been active in the field of the environment, and has recently launched a new initiative to promote the use of renewable energy sources. why would you do that? because those member states which have so far helped to block such authorisations may decide to drop their resistance at community level, since they can exercise their right to ban gmo crops at national level. it's not the ideal scenario, but it's an improvement on the current situation.
in writing. genetically modified organisms (gmos) are a danger to the environment and human health. it seems to me fair that member states should be able to restrict and even prohibit the cultivation of gmos on their territory. it would also seem fair to me to implement a financial liability mechanism for compensation in case of accidents/contamination of organic crops. in this respect, i regret that the necessary support for the implementation of such measures has not been given at the level of the european parliament. on the other hand, this report envisages the introduction of border co-existence measures against crop contamination - measures that benefit member states and, by implication, farmers, with a view to organic agri-food products. it does not seem logical to me that biotech companies should be involved, or rather play such a strong role, in the authorisation phase of the cultivation of genetically modified products. there should be no attempt to equate governments/member states with biotech companies. it is nevertheless positive that the negotiations have succeeded in reducing the role of these companies in the first phase of the authorisation of gmo cultivation. i would like to congratulate the rapporteur on her report and hope that we will have the support of our colleagues for the compromise package we have achieved.
in writing. i voted in favour of this recommendation because the agreement strengthens cooperation between the european union and the democratic republic of são tomé and príncipe with a view to establishing a sustainable fisheries policy and the rational exploitation of fisheries resources, in the interests of both parties. the agreement also provides for the possibility for european union vessels to fish in são toméan waters in accordance with available scientific advice and the recommendations of the international commission for the conservation of atlantic tunas. i believe that the european union countries will benefit from this agreement and that the effects will be positive and long-lasting.
in writing. i voted in favour of this project as the cooperation between the european union and the democratic republic of são tomé and príncipe is long-standing. this project is useful for the fishing industry, but we must nevertheless ensure that the negative results of previous collaborations will not be repeated in the future.
in writing. i voted in favour of this resolution because i consider that this agreement is nothing but a continuation of the protocol already concluded by the two parties in 2013 for a certain period and which has now expired. at present, vessels flying the flag of seychelles may fish in mayotte waters only on the basis of an agreement between the prefect of mayotte and vessels flying the flag of seychelles. the agreement will therefore allow seychelles vessels to continue to have access to mayotte's waters and to marine biological resources under the jurisdiction of the european union.
in writing. i voted in favour of this agreement because it is mutually beneficial, favours the economic development of mayotte and seychelles and complies with the rules of the common fisheries policy and the iotc rules on conservation of resources.
in writing. on 23 october 2006, the council authorised the commission, on behalf of the european community and its member states, to negotiate with tunisia a protocol amending the agreements concluded between the european community and third countries, and in particular the euro-mediterranean association agreement between the european communities and their member states, of the one part, and tunisia, of the other part, to take account of the accession of the new member states, namely romania and bulgaria, to the eu. the treaty concerning the accession of bulgaria and romania to the european union entered into force on 1 january 2007, and the protocol must now take account of the accession of those two states to the eu. i voted in favour of this recommendation primarily because their country of origin is covered by this protocol and the fulfilment of all aspects of the country's full integration is an objective for both romania and the european union.
in writing. i voted in favour of this protocol as romania supports the existing cooperation under the euro-mediterranean agreement between the european commission and tunisia. tunisia is a country in the process of democratization and the experience of romania can be used by the european union in supporting the democratic transition in this country.
in writing. the amendment of directive 2001/18 is intended to increase the degree of decision-making of the member states on the cultivation of genetically modified organisms on their territory. more flexibility is needed in this respect, taking into account national or regional characteristics regarding the use of agricultural land. at the same time, member states should be able to assess the risks and impact of gmos on citizens, the environment and animal health. i voted in favour of amending the directive because i believe that the member states are in a position to take responsibility for their authorisation and cultivation. impartial studies are also needed to strengthen scientific knowledge on genetically modified organisms. their long-term environmental impact is less well known, so i believe that the development of impact studies and the information derived from them should be made available to consumers. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of genetically modified organisms (gmos) in food and feed. we need very clear boundaries for the areas to be used for gmo cultivation. the authorisation of these areas must take into account the adjacent agricultural crops in order to avoid contamination.
in writing. the new legislation, adopted today at second reading after being blocked in the council for four years, will allow member states to restrict or completely ban crops containing genetically modified organisms (gmos) on their territory, even if they are allowed at eu level. i support this agreement because it will provide more flexibility for member states who want to restrict the cultivation of gmos on their territory for reasons of environmental protection, as well as urban or national planning, socioeconomic impact or agricultural policy objectives.
in writing. this is a highly sensitive and controversial subject, which has been in the political and legislative debate since the beginning of the barroso ii commission. in the context of a permanent deadlock at council level, it is ultimately a common sense solution to give member states the opportunity to decide whether or not to accept gmo crops. it will be important that the rules for coexistence of gmo crops with other 'normal' crops are sound, to prevent 'infestation' of classic crops with genetics from genetically modified ones. the decision does not change the rules of international trade in any way: genetically modified soybeans, for example, can be imported into the eu as before. the only change is that the member states, not brussels, either the council or the commission, will have the hardest say in the decision to approve the cultivation, after the eu's specialised agency decides that, scientifically speaking, the crops are ok from the point of view of consumer health, other plants, etc.
in writing. i voted in favour of this draft legislation which gives member states the possibility to restrict or prohibit the cultivation of gmos on their territory. the draft legislation aims to complement the existing regulatory framework on gmos to allow member states to restrict or prohibit the cultivation of gmos on their territory. the proposed measures concern only the cultivation of gmos and the scientifically based eu-wide gmo authorisation system remains unchanged. the legislative proposal responds to the member states' request for more freedom in the application of a national gmo cultivation policy, both to member states interested in restricting and to those interested in cultivating gmos at national level.
in writing. i consider this a useful step in unblocking the european decision-making process in the discussions of recent years on the authorisation process for gmos at european level, given that the legislative proposal is only about responding to the request from the member states of the european union to be able to restrict or prohibit, as appropriate, the cultivation of a gmo crop and does not change the european authorisation system in any way. they argue that romania should be able to decide independently of other countries whether it wants to restrict or ban a gmo crop. the fact that member states that will grow gmos will be obliged to take measures to avoid cross-border contamination must also be considered as respecting the decision of other states that decide differently.
in writing. i welcome the decision of the european parliament and of the council to amend regulation (eu) no 1343/2011 of the european parliament and of the council of 13 december 2011 on certain provisions relating to fishing in the gfcm (general fisheries commission for the mediterranean) agreement area. i consider that there is a need to update the existing provisions by including the measures contained in the cgpm recommendations. these technical sustainable exploitation measures based on the gfcm recommendations confirm the gfcm's main objective of maintaining a good ecological status of the mediterranean sea basin and are in line with the new common fisheries policy, which aims mainly to lay the foundations for economically, socially and environmentally sustainable fisheries. the proposal is important because it represents an improvement on existing fisheries provisions at eu level. in recent years, the commission has played an important role in encouraging the cgpm to take initiatives that allow for the establishment of an effective management framework, and this needs to be sustained.
in writing. i voted in favour of the report as the proposal aims at transposing into union law several measures adopted by the general fisheries commission for the mediterranean (gfcm) at its annual sessions in 2011, 2012 and 2013. the gfcm is a regional fisheries management organisation established under article xiv of the fao constitution. the eu and 10 member states (bulgaria, croatia, cyprus, france, greece, italy, malta, slovenia, spain and romania) are contracting parties to the gfcm agreement. to the extent that the content of the gfcm recommendations is not or only partially reflected in existing union legislation, the transposition of the relevant provisions of the gfcm is necessary to ensure that it is applied uniformly and effectively throughout the european union.

in writing. the european union is discussing a new security policy today, in the wake of the absolutely abominable terrorist attack in paris. in the european context, it is the duty of the european institutions to move to the stage of concrete action in the light of the new terrorist threats emanating from the territory of the member states themselves. we are now talking about an internal threat that requires extremely close, coherent and effective cooperation between all 28 states. with romania having the longest external eu border in eastern europe, schengen membership, postponed for political and not technical reasons, becomes crucial. security measures must be increased at the eu's external borders and the movement within these borders of individuals belonging to terrorist organisations must be even more closely monitored. romania's accession to schengen can only bring more expertise in preventing and combating terrorist activities in the eu. romania's accession to schengen thus becomes beneficial not only to romanian citizens and romanian companies, but to the entire european union. with an active conflict on the eu's eastern border, romania, the safety of all europeans would increase if this border became the schengen border.
in writing. on 3 january 2015, the deadliest attack in the history of the boko haram terrorist group took place, killing 2,000 people in nigeria, mostly women, children and elderly people who could not flee, in an attack on baga, near the border with chad. it's well known that boko haram is an extremist islamist group that believes education and books should be banned, killing over 10,000 people last year alone. nigeria's president goodluck jonathan, who has spoken out about the paris attacks, has not commented on the atrocities in his own country. even as nigeria prepares for presidential and parliamentary elections next month, i find it unimaginable that you want to maintain your image at the expense of peace and security, and the fight against terrorism is becoming virtually impossible. i believe that european states with economic interests in the area should have a constructive and effective dialogue with the nigerian authorities in order to fight terrorism and to ensure respect for the fundamental rights of citizens. it is also important that the western press has access to sources of information precisely so that these atrocities are brought to the attention of the international world to be condemned and the necessary support provided to be fought.

mr president, i am very pleased that 2015 has been dedicated to the issue of development, and especially about its timing. 2015 will be a year of important negotiations on how to tackle global poverty. the un climate change conference in paris next november is one of the most important of these. this is because climate change threatens to undermine decades of development and puts future development trajectories at risk. many of the main drivers behind poverty in developing countries are intertwined with climate change. increased drought, for example, leads to crop failure and food insecurity, reduces opportunities and boosts inequality around the world. when dealing with the issue of development, we should strongly promote environmental initiatives, energy efficiency, exchange of technologies and best practices, investment in public education and in disaster risk reduction and, more generally, emphasise low carbon emission development. developing countries will bear the brunt of the effects of climate change as they strive to overcome poverty and achieve economic growth. in fact, one of the top priorities of the european union development agenda is to achieve accomplishment of the cop 21 negotiations in paris.
in the context of the european year of development, i believe it is important to stress that the european union and its member states, as well as the world's largest donor, should pay greater attention to the promotion of human rights than they do at present. of course, humanitarian emergencies require rapid intervention, but we must also promote in development policy those aspects which are intended to promote the protection of human rights. i am convinced that europe must not only be at the forefront of traditional humanitarian aid, but also help these societies through the sustainable and integrated development of the developing world economy. i think it is extraordinary that this year, through the themes broken down by month, we are bringing the attention of europeans to the most pressing problems facing our world. the words education, health, migration, food security mean something completely different in less developed parts of the world than they do in our own.
in writing. – in 2015 we are launching the year of development, and major challenges lie ahead. the eu has to intervene where it is needed and where it can make a difference. eu development policy is a centrepiece of the union’s relationship with the outside world. with 50% of all global development aid, the eu is the world’s leading donor. now we need to define the post-2015 agenda. the overarching goal is the eradication of poverty. while the proportion of people living in extreme poverty has dropped, there are many who still live below the internationally defined poverty line. the new framework should provide for improved living standards, access to primary healthcare systems, free education and improvements in agriculture and, above all, for the existence of basic fundamental rights. working with developing nations and emerging economies should create a win-win situation.
in writing. the european year for development should be a moment to raise awareness of the need for the european union to get involved in solving the problems of underdevelopment around the world. eu member states have committed to the millennium development goals, but unfortunately have not kept their political or financial commitments. we are far from the financial target of 0.7% of gnp allocated to development cooperation by the member countries and still further from the development criteria by the poor countries. the eu and its member states must take advantage of the european year for development to put international development back on the public agenda. i assure you of my full support as a member of the european parliament and as a university academic specialising in this field, and i am sure that many europeans, many of them young, are eager to get involved in supporting a europe that is a leader in international assistance and cooperation.
in writing. – eradicating poverty in developing countries is an important priority for the eu. our efforts should go hand in hand with those aiming for the achievement of the sustainable development goals. i welcome the european year for development initiative and i am convinced that an integrated european approach together with the involvement with the various stakeholders will result in significant progress. instability and conflict situations are unfortunately typical for the less developed areas in africa, south america and asia and in many cases violent conflicts and illegal activities of local militias are financed from mineral extraction and trade. breaking the link between mineral extraction and conflict financing is a complex challenge. the european parliament is taking the lead in the eu action to promote responsible behaviour by companies operating in such areas. an integrated approach is entailing a trade-related eu regulation but also foreign policy action and development cooperation initiatives. as the rapporteur for the regulation setting up an eu system for supply chain due diligence self-certification of importers of 3tg originating in conflict-affected and high-risk areas i am committed to contributing to the elaboration and adoption of an efficient and balanced regulation at the core of the eu integrated approach.
vice-president of the commission / high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. - mr president, on the situation in egypt, this is a time that is quite symbolic. if we look back exactly four years ago, egypt was on the brink of the 25 january revolution, with people taking to the streets calling for dignity, social justice and simply bread – their legitimate political and socio-economic rights. ever since, the european union has stood by egypt and its people, fully supporting these democratic demands. today, four years later, egypt is still in political transition. eighteen months after the ousting of president morsi, egypt is still in transition pending the parliamentary elections planned to start at the end of march, which will be a crucial step in concluding the constitutional roadmap. two steps have been achieved. egypt has given itself a constitution and it has elected a new president. both steps were monitored by the european union with the mission for the presidential elections in may. a delegation of the european parliament was part of it. now we would like to see the mission recommendations taken on board, particularly in view of the upcoming parliamentary elections. difficulties, however, remain, and i have decided not to send a fully-fledged observation mission this time but, instead, to deploy a smaller expert mission (eem). the purpose of the mission is closely to assess and report on the electoral process, including on the political environment and electoral campaign. the list of recommendations to be drawn up by this mission will facilitate constructive engagement with the authorities on much-needed reform efforts. but democracy goes beyond elections, and we all know that very well here. a parliament is key to having a legitimate legislator in place to tackle the many tasks of urgent legislative reform – including the law on ngos and the controversial protest law – and to ensure compliance with the new constitution, which will need to be implemented. the parliamentary elections are also an important step towards providing a broad base for political engagement that can ensure fundamental rights and freedoms, security and economic reform accepted by the whole of society. open political engagement and discussion will reduce the risk of radicalisation. another challenge is clearly that of the deteriorating security situation spreading beyond the sinai. we have always affirmed that the european union stands by egypt in fighting terrorism. there is no place for violence. the special coordinator for counterterrorism travelled to egypt in december 2014, and we are looking now into possibilities of holding a dialogue on counterterrorism and security. let me add that this is not only in egypt’s interest but also in our own european union interest. seeing the fragility, to say the least, of the situation in the whole region, we welcome and have welcomed egypt’s re-emergence as an important regional player. in particular, the role that the country played over the summer in reaching a ceasefire in gaza, facilitating the israeli-palestinian talks, and then more recently with the conference for reconstruction in gaza that was held in cairo in the autumn, was very important. furthermore, egypt is re-emerging as an important foreign policy player in the league of arab states, in the african union and in sub-saharan africa, in particular over the nile water issues with ethiopia and in national dialogue efforts with sudan. while still in political transition and facing security threats, egypt also urgently needs to tackle an economic situation that is particularly difficult. steps taken by the new authorities go in the right direction, with subsidy cuts and large-scale infrastructure projects such as the new lane in the suez canal. the eu will continue to support egypt in addressing its socio-economic reforms. we will participate in the international investment conference planned for march. we will continue to focus our support in the socio-economic field, to help improve living conditions for the most vulnerable among egypt’s population. these challenges and the ongoing political transition cannot allow any compromise on human rights. egypt needs to address its human rights situation, including the lack of political space for dissenting opinion and shrinking space for freedoms of assembly and expression. too many of the issues that you mentioned in your resolution on freedom of expression and assembly in egypt last july have not yet been addressed. only last december we saw another decision by a court to pass preliminary death sentences on 188 defendants. we keep calling on the judicial authorities to respect due process and ensure fair trial. a truly professional and independent judiciary is a key element for functioning and trusted state institutions. another concern – a deep concern, as we have said in statements – is the lack of accountability and the continued crackdown not only on the muslim brotherhood and affiliates but also on political opponents and liberal activists, illustrated by often disproportionate sentencing. there are too many civilians tried by military courts, and too often, laws such as the new draft anti-terrorism law and the existing ngo law, which does not comply with the new constitution, give too ample a degree of discretion to the executive. we keep addressing these issues when we meet with our egyptian counterparts. in particular, i have to thank the special representative for human rights, stavros lambrinidis, a former colleague of some of you, who repeatedly raised these issues with the egyptian authorities on the occasion of both of his visits to egypt during 2014. the question for the eu is not whether we should support egypt – there is no other option but to stay engaged with egypt – but how best to support its transition. therefore egypt, like all our southern and eastern partners, will be closely involved in the review of the european neighbourhood policy (enp). the outdated action plan with egypt will need to be re-negotiated, taking into account the enp review and to better reflect the reality on the ground. we will monitor the parliamentary elections with our experts, as i said, and we will monitor the further implementation of the constitution and, with a view to the upcoming parliamentary elections, the freedom of the press and media. but we will also help egypt with its economic reform efforts and its fight against security threats. we will work with egypt too in the context of our own efforts and our own fight against our own security threats.

2013, which is now two years ago. so, if you want to hold us accountable, also hold us accountable on our actions. i am glad to be accountable in that respect, and i would actually urge this at european level. there are many member states where the levels of transparency and accountability are not the same as in the commission and the other eu institutions, but still i do acknowledge that ombudsman. - madam president, honourable members, i would like to thank you all very much for your contributions and the thought that you have brought to them. i take everything that you say on board. i take the compliments, obviously, but i also take the criticism because, without feedback from you, who are even closer to the people than i am, i cannot really know what their true concerns are. i see you as a very valuable resource in relation to that. there were many issues raised, and obviously i cannot deal on an individual basis with all of them, although of course you are more than welcome to come to me as individual meps and discuss any matter that you want. but there are a number of general issues that i want to discuss. a lot of you talked about the visibility of the office. i hope that i am demonstrating that this is certainly a priority for me and that, if people do not know that i am here, the service that i can provide for them is fairly redundant. i have made a very big effort to make the office more visible through a number of techniques. what is also very important – and some of you have alluded to this – is your own national ombudsmen, member state ombudsmen, the petitions committee or regional ombudsmen and the work that i can do to improve that. as you probably know, as european ombudsman, i chair the european network of ombudsmen, and just yesterday i had a strategy meeting in relation to how they can help me. equally i can also help them with their own situations. two of the things i am doing include, for the first time next year, producing an annual report on the work of the network, in which i will highlight not just my own work but also the work of the member state ombudsmen. hopefully, if they agree with this, then they too can present commission and the agencies. i set my own challenges as well. right from the start, i have said that the compliance rate of 80% + is not high enough, because in many member states, including my own – ireland – the compliance rate for the recommendations of the ombudsman is often as high as 95% or even 100%. that is a very high target, but it is one that i will strive to achieve. in relation to effectiveness, a lot of you have pointed to the fact that many of the complaints that come before me are outside of my remit. obviously most complaints that european citizens have are with their member states, but one of the functions of the office is to be as helpful as possible and to direct anybody who comes to us to where they can have their problem resolved. but this is partly why i have begun to focus very intensively on the own-initiative investigations, to see what systemic issues i can deal with which my office and the resources that i have can add greatest value to. i suppose my overall ambition for the office is simply to be useful – more useful to the citizen, more useful to parliament, more useful to the commission and so on. to do that, i need to collaborate with you. you have to support me if you find that my recommendations are rational and that you wish to support them, because without your help i cannot succeed as i might. i also need to collaborate well with the commission and with the agencies. they have to trust me, just as the citizens have to trust me. so i thank you all for your contributions. i will take them on board. i just want to make one point about the troika. many people have come to me over the last year to see what i can do to investigate the troika. the troika is not an eu body per se, even though the ecb and the eu commission are critical parts of it. what i have said to individual meps is that, if they wish to work with me and if there is a particular issue or facet of the work of the troika, as it relates to an eu institution, that they feel i could legitimately investigate, then that is something that i would be very happy to do. at the moment, as the irish members know, there is an investigation into the banking collapse and the financial crisis in ireland. they are trying to get the ecb over to explain itself to the irish people, and we will see how that evolves. thank you all very much for your contributions and your support.

and better support for the council of europe in these efforts. all relevant instruments should be fully mobilized to respond to human rights violations. we will be looking forward to forthcoming the next item is the debate on seven motions for resolutions on pakistan, in particular the situation following the peshawar school attack.
vice-president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs. - madam president, thank you for this debate that i think helps us to focus on a couple of important points after the terrible attack by the pakistani taliban against the school in peshawar on 16 december. first of all, there is the fact that the attack was deliberately against children – boys and girls. but it was also an attack against the right to education for every boy and girl. as many of you said, not only the sakharov prize but also the nobel peace prize going to malala yousafzai was a strong reaction to that. let me say that the best news we have had, in reaction to what happened, was the re-opening of the school in peshawar this week. i think this is the strongest sign of the fact that the right to education of girls and boys cannot be stopped by such terrible attacks. the second thing that this attack reminded us of – and someone mentioned this – is the fact that the first victims of terrorists are muslims. yesterday we discussed nigeria and today we are discussing pakistan. i think part of our counter-terrorist measures is the narrative and the awareness that it is not only us we care about, but it is also about all others. pakistan has paid a high price to terrorism and extremism, with up to 50 000 people killed by terrorists since 2001. a new comprehensive national action plan has been approved. key elements include regulating madrasas, blocking financing mechanisms of terrorist organisations, and measures against religious persecution. we have set up a specific eu-pakistan political dialogue on counter-terrorism, the priorities of which are the rule of law and anti-radicalisation. the eu, through a number of different projects, already supports the pakistani government’s counter-terrorism activities aimed at reducing the threat from militant groups operating in the territory. this includes support for capacity-building of law enforcement, community policing, promoting dialogue between different communities and strengthening resilience to violence. but, as many of you have said today, counter-terrorism alone does not stand. we have to start from the root causes and from prevention. in 2008 pakistan started its transition from military rule to democracy. in 2013 the country experienced its first ever handing-over of power from one democratically-elected government to another. the eu has consistently supported the democratisation process. our election observation missions were in pakistan in 2008 and 2013. the transition to civilian democracy led to closer eu cooperation with pakistan in different fields and to a more structured partnership, including political dialogue on sensitive and complicated issues like human rights and counter-terrorism. let me stress this, because it is also a coherent part of our work on security, disarmament and non-proliferation, especially in a region crucial for peace and security. the key priorities in our human rights engagement and dialogue with pakistan – and let me remind you that the eu special representative for human rights, stavros lambrinidis, made his first ever visit to pakistan this year – include freedom of religion and belief, women’s rights, the death penalty and the rule of law and access to justice. the issue of religious minorities remains a central aspect of our human rights dialogue. freedom of religion and expression are constitutional rights in pakistan, but discrimination remains, severely affecting, for instance, shias and ahmadis, but also christians and other minorities. the use of the blasphemy law has become a reason for particular concern. the overwhelming majority of cases are filed against muslims, but christians are also targeted – such as in the case of asia bibi, which i know this parliament has been following particularly closely. let me say that i am following it closely with you. pakistan needs to strengthen civilian courts and institutions. the judicial system has to be adequately resourced, trained and equipped, in order to deal effectively with terrorism. harsher punishments or the temporary expansion of the jurisdiction of military courts do not address a weak judicial system. developing an effective, efficient, professional, independent and credible civilian legal system remains a key priority for pakistan, and the eu is ready to support and train police, prosecutors, defence lawyers and judges. after peshawar – as some of you mentioned – pakistan also lifted the de facto moratorium on executions that had been in place since 2008. let me conclude by saying that the european union remains – and will remain – opposed to the death penalty in all circumstances. the death penalty is not an effective tool in the fight against terrorism, and i sincerely hope that the moratorium will be re-established.

in writing. the european parliament's motion for a resolution on the dramatic situation in libya, which has experienced a succession of political, institutional and security crises since the fall of gaddafi in 2011, draws attention to the recent events of the abduction of 20 egyptian christians and the violence of dozens of militias that have spiralled out of control. unfortunately, the aspirations of the libyan people, which emerged from the 2011 revolution, have been replaced by a power vacuum, and this situation has given rise to several militias running their own territories, and successive governments in tripoli can barely enforce their authority. some of the tragedies that are happening in the mediterranean, such as the proliferation of smuggling networks and where entire ships of migrants are abandoned by their original crews, have their roots both in the wars in syria and iraq and in libya's inability to control its borders. this appeal to the international community once again underlines the imminent danger posed by the terrorist bases developing in libya to the surrounding countries and to europe.

in writing. — four years after taking to the streets for dignity, freedom and democracy and the tragic experience of state repression which ultimately led to the ousting of the gaddafi regime, libyans find themselves today in a country characterised by political division and violence, with the risk of further escalation to an outright civil war. the intensification of the crisis has heavily affected the population, with civilian suffering, casualties, mass displacement and a spreading humanitarian crisis. the un-brokered talks in geneva represent a last chance. all parties to the conflict are called upon to make the only possible step for peace: that of freezing all military operations as proposed by un special representative leon in order to create an inclusive environment conducive to maximum restraint, national dialogue and reconciliation. there is no military solution to the current conflict, and an unconditional ceasefire is the only possible response to the suffering of the libyan population. the european union stands ready to provide the necessary support. it is the last opportunity for peace. this is the rationale of this week’s new round of political dialogue scheduled to take place in geneva. this is the call the european parliament makes by adopting this resolution.

in writing. the economic crisis has affected most economic sectors, with the consequences being increased unemployment, decreased productivity and profitability in certain sectors. the post-crisis 'hangover' effect has led to a sharp decline in investment at eu level, which has contributed to a decline in confidence and created a relative uncertainty about the european economic climate. we need financial instruments to stimulate private investment and guarantee its implementation. private capital intervention in public investment will mean more efficient and responsible spending. the outcome of the greek elections created new fears and immediately affected financial markets, with effects that are subsequently reflected in the economies of the member states. i am convinced that the european fund for strategic investments (efsi) will play a role in reducing these fears and in strengthening investor confidence in the eu's economic potential. by attracting private capital into the economy and guaranteeing investments, the new investment strategy brings multiple benefits: it guarantees investments by facilitating access to credit, contributes to the development of smes through job creation and generates long-term investment. at the same time, i believe that any possible additional contribution of more than 8 billion from the eu budget should be excluded from discussion.
in writing. with the highest unemployment rate in the eu (26% and rising to 51% among young people), almost a third of the population excluded from public health care and below the poverty line, including 40% pension cuts, a gdp per capita 30% below 2008 levels and a record eu public debt equivalent to 175% of national gdp, greece is exhausted by the crisis, austerity and impoverishment. the outcome of the legislative elections is a wake-up call in this regard. the huge sums spent by international creditors on greece alone, as well as the painful social costs, show how much investment, coordinated at european level, is needed in the equation to break out of stagnation. i believe that compliance with greece's commitments on fiscal responsibility and a realistic assessment of the country's ability to repay its debts can provide a basis for investment-based recovery. the increasingly desperate situation in greece is a warning sign of the economic future of a european union that is failing to find the pace of growth it needs. i therefore believe that the strategic investment fund should focus on channelling liquidity to the countries and sectors most affected by the crisis.

in writing. – considering the 23 million unemployed in the european union, expectations are justifiably high regarding the juncker commission’s eur 15 billion investment plan to put europe back on a growth track and create new jobs. i believe that, in order to achieve good results with the investment plan, we must follow two rules from the outset. first, we should ensure that enough money is targeted towards countries where there is insufficient credit for smes, thereby creating more impact where this money is truly needed. second, with regard to the project selection criteria, we should ensure that these are clear enough and that they allow for competitiveness between projects, but, at the same time, that they lead to the financing not of deadweight projects that would have been financed anyway but of projects with a high leverage effect conducive to the creation of jobs which would not have been created in the absence of the financing. we should also use this tool to support investment in novel and high-risk areas like green energy and the digital economy, where investment is truly needed and where we can have a strong impact in terms of the realisation of the eu 2020 strategy.
in writing. i welcome the european commission's focus on implementing the investment programme through the european fund for strategic investments (efsi) as soon as possible. i appreciate the conceptual construction of this fund and the fact that member states can participate in the formation of the capital needed for the fund, and this effort will be taken into account in the budget deficit analysis. i believe that both potential private investors and beneficiaries of investments want to know more details about the mechanism of formation of the financing costs. it is important that the efsi contributes to achieving a reasonable balance between the desire of investors for the highest possible return and the desire of the beneficiaries of investments that need the lowest possible cost of funding.

all the polls show that europeans want to know where the food they eat comes from. one reason is the desire to buy local products to support local producers. another may be trying to avoid food brought from thousands of miles away because of the huge impact on the environment. there are people who want to know details about the origin of food for religious reasons. however, clearly the main factor influencing this decision is cost, and the labelling requirements and in particular the requirement to specify the country of origin of the food were said to lead to an increase in prices. the commission certainly needs to look very carefully at this impact of labelling regulations. so far, the commission's studies have been based on reports from the food industry. however, there are also external studies that indicate different results. we need a much more serious analysis of the potential costs before we deny consumers the right to be informed. we already have rules that require country of origin labelling for fresh meat, and we have traceability systems for food safety reasons. so the systems already exist and are functional. i therefore do not think that an increase in food prices would be justified if this information were also communicated to consumers through labels.
food safety and traceability of food products and food by-products must be top priorities for authorities at european and national level. practice has shown us, however, that simply labelling the country of origin or place of origin of meat does not prevent fraud in the food sector or improve food safety. such regulation would only increase the level of information of citizens. i support a voluntary system of labelling the origin of ingredients in meat products which allows member states to opt for the introduction of such regulation. both at national and european level, there are authorities responsible for ensuring product traceability to ensure consumer safety, and we need to ensure that these institutions function effectively. in some countries, like my own, where purchasing power is reduced because of low incomes, where small and medium-sized enterprises producing consumer products represent a large part of the food sector, it is difficult to talk about such regulation which can bring an additional administrative burden as well as higher manufacturing costs, and therefore, by implication, higher costs of food products consumed by citizens. my personal position, which is the same as that of romania and the majority of the group to which i belong, is to maintain the current voluntary labelling system.
in writing. the first objective of food labelling is to provide consistent and transparent information so that the consumer can make an informed choice. many european companies are responding to this expectation by providing information on the origin of the product as a voluntary practice. a 'one size fits all' approach, requiring mandatory labelling of the origin of meat used as an ingredient in processed foods would have severe negative consequences for food manufacturers, farmers, retailers and consumers, create significant supply chain problems, lead to possible disruption and major inefficiencies, with the potential to increase consumer prices and food waste. all of this could result in a less competitive european food chain. as regards the consumer, a balanced measure must be identified to ensure that the consumer is informed, but without significant increases in the prices of meat products and without increasing the administrative burden for both the authorities and the agro-industrial operators, who are already facing financial difficulties due to the economic crisis.
in writing. – origin labelling provides consumers with the possibility to make informed choices about the food they wish to purchase and consume. consumers’ interest in the origin of their food has grown over the years, meat products being no exception, as most studies show that the origin of meat is usually in the top five aspects influencing purchase options. origin labelling for foodstuffs with meat as an ingredient would answer concerns related to food quality, food safety, and animal welfare, but also economic and environmental concerns. considering that, compared to the eu/non-eu labelling option only specific country of origin labelling could provide meaningful information, it is only in the latter case that introducing new labelling measures would make sense. nevertheless, considering the anticipated costs associated with such measures, maybe the commission should explore the possibility of limiting the scope of application of such a labelling measure so as to ensure that consumers have enough information, but at the same time producers would not have to bear an excessive burden.

the cross-border exchange of information on traffic offences goes beyond the scope of mere police cooperation and is part of a much larger objective, namely road safety, which is a political priority of the european parliament. this proposal for a directive brings us one step closer to the objective of reducing the number of road deaths by around 50% by 2020. the adoption of this initiative is a mission we owe to those we represent who face every day an outdated fleet of vehicles and undeveloped infrastructure, due to the drastic reduction in maintenance costs and the lack of funding for related improvement works. in a european union built on the freedom of citizens to move easily and safely within the territory of the member states, cross-border exchange of information and cooperation between the authorities of these states are essential in discouraging traffic offences by motorists.

in writing. there are frequent situations where a european legislative act has been amended several times over the years. this creates a difficulty for the european citizen who will ultimately fail to understand what the essence of the legislative act is and which of the existing amendments is the one in force. the european commission, which has the right to initiate and propose draft legislation, has always taken on board and advocated the need for simple and clear legislation so that every european citizen can understand the legislative act and make use of the specific rights conferred on him by it. clarification of european legislation is done through a legislative procedure called codification of legislation. in order to ensure the rapid adoption of consolidated acts, the european institutions agreed in 1994 to use an accelerated procedure. the legislative proposal which was the subject of the european parliament's report concerns the codification of council regulation (ec) no 1061/2009 of 19 october 2009 establishing a common export regime. since the proposal for codification preserves the content of the codified acts in full and only makes changes in form, the european parliament, by its unanimous vote today, supports the proposal for the codification of the regulation.
in writing. i voted in favour of the report on the proposal for a council decision on the declaration by the member states, in the interest of the european union, of acceptance of gabon's accession to the 1980 hague convention on the civil aspects of international child abduction. the gabonese state deposited its instrument of accession to the 1980 convention on 6 december 2010 and the convention entered into force on 1 march 2011. the convention, which has been ratified by 86 countries to date, including all eu member states, is a measure of cooperation in international law. the convention merely provides the necessary balance between the interests of the individual and those of society in order to enforce the right to the immediate return of the illegally removed or retained child in harmony with the right to respect for family life. child safety measures are welcome, as citizens can now be protected from the dangers of child abuse.
in writing. — i strongly support the adoption of stronger cooperative measures to prevent cases of international child abduction. greater coordination between states is necessary to avoid the temptation, by one of the parents, to secure custody of a child following a separation or a divorce. the hague convention of 25 october 1980 makes it possible to resolve, at an international level, those cases in which the courts of both of the states concerned declare themselves competent and award custody of the child to the parent who is a national of their state. moreover the convention introduces a system which ensures the immediate return of abducted children. i welcome the accession of gabon to the hague convention. considering the number of eu citizens of gabonese origin, this accession is vital to ensure eu-wide protection of the children in question.
