president. - the next item is the debate on the question with a request for an oral answer on maternity leave, to the council and the commission by arena maria and iratxe garcía pérez, on behalf of the committee on women's rights and gender equality (hyperlink "http://www.europarl.europa.eu). the commission notes that the commission has not provided any evidence that the aid is compatible with the internal market. the commission shall be empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with article 26 to supplement this regulation by laying down detailed rules for the application of this regulation.
president-in-office of the council.– mr president, i would like to thank you for this opportunity to address the state of play as regards the commission’s proposal to revise the maternity leave directive. during the past few months, the presidency has met with parliament’s representatives on several occasions to discuss this subject. as you know, the commission has expressed its intention to withdraw the proposal if there is no tangible progress on unblocking the negotiations by the summer. i shall be very honest with you: the proposal as it stands clearly does not enjoy support in the council. the council’s position does not leave any room for further manoeuvre. we must also be realistic about the fact that parliament’s position on, and expectations from, the proposal are fundamentally different from the council’s. we respect that stance. however, we must face the fact that the current state of affairs will not allow us to progress on the issue. allow me to stress one thing: the council’s position was not arrived at easily. it is the result of profound and complex reflection. tremendous effort and good will was invested by the previous presidencies. the presidency cannot act on its own: it is bound by the will of the member states, just as the parliament is bound by the will of its members. despite the difficulties that have surrounded this issue, i believe that the council and parliament remain united in their commitment to advancing the well—being of europe’s women – and of working mothers in particular. the council has repeatedly stressed the importance of supporting women and men in the struggle to reconcile work, family and private life. promoting women’s full participation in the labour market is not only a matter of equality but also an important factor contributing to overall economic growth. with that overall objective in mind, after seven years of efforts that have not brought us to an agreement, we would very much welcome a fresh start on this subject. a new initiative would provide a better basis for the council and parliament to work jointly towards improving the reconciliation of work and family life, for both women and men. this should, of course, include the protection of pregnant and breastfeeding women. i hope that parliament will be able to share the council’s view on the need to take a more comprehensive and forward-looking approach. thank you for your attention.
member of the commission.– mr president, i would like to thank the committee on women’s rights and gender equality (femm) for their engagement and especially for their efforts in relation to the commission’s proposal to revise the maternity leave directive. in particular i would like to pay tribute to the rapporteur, mrs arena, and to the chair of the femm committee, mrs garcía pérez, and to their efforts to find a way out of the stalemate. the commission is strongly committed to gender equality and the protection of pregnant women and new mothers. the commission recognises the need for women and men to be able to balance working life so they can combine it with their family life. the commission has stressed on many occasions its readiness to facilitate negotiations between parliament and the council. we have engaged in continuous efforts to break the deadlock. my services have worked closely with previous and current presidencies and with this house to try to find a realistic solution acceptable to both sides. thanks to mrs arena, we recently had the opportunity to explore new possibilities for compromise, particularly on the question of pay, which we know was difficult for member states in times of economic crisis. the commission has facilitated informal talks between parliament and the council, requested a discussion in the council and has advocated concrete discussions on the basis of the rapporteur’s proposals in order to move towards an agreement. we have insisted that the presidency bring this back for discussion in the council on the basis of the rapporteur’s proposals in order to unblock the negotiations and try to move towards an agreement. when the file came back to the council at political level recently, the commission recalled parliament’s position and readiness to engage. unfortunately, a solid group of member states remains opposed to any further negotiations on this file. many of them agree that there is a strong case for action in this field, but they are not convinced that this proposal, preparations for which started almost 10 years ago, will solve the issues faced by working parents in 2015 and beyond. overall, there is a majority in favour of a fresh start in the council. i remain open to continued discussion with the co-legislators, but as things stand now the commission sees no reason to depart from its intention, as announced in the work programme, to withdraw the proposal and replace it with a new initiative if no agreement can be found within six months. a fresh start now appears likely to be the best way forward. society and the labour market have undergone significant changes in the recent period. the commission is committed to improving the situation of working parents in the eu. i am therefore open to start looking into a new approach to tackle the challenges faced by them. we know that it is mainly women who are hit by what the economists call ‘the motherhood penalty’. they see their potential, and even their ability to participate in the labour market, fall when they become parents. the gender pay gap, which is almost non-existent before child-bearing age, remains, still, at 16% and the gender pension gap stands at 39%. at the same time, we know that europe faces a demographic time bomb that risks becoming a serious economic and social problem, as well as a fiscal problem for the eu, and as the economy starts to pick up, europe needs to make best use of all our talents to compete in the global marketplace. women are more highly qualified than ever before, more highly qualified on average than men. we cannot afford to continue to neglect this talent pool at a time of shrinking populations and growing worldwide competition. women and men have to be able to balance working life so that they can have the family they want. they need to have a choice. men should also be encouraged to live up to their family responsibilities. many men would like to spend more time with their children but face difficult circumstances in the workplace. creating conditions that allow a proper work-life balance will help families, businesses and our societies as a whole and will promote more gender equality at all levels. the challenges for working parents start with the arrival of a new baby, but they do not end there. parents also need a certain level of flexibility throughout the childhood and teenage years. there needs to be a decent level of childcare and care-services infrastructure in place to give people a meaningful choice, and we must not forget the challenges of caring for elderly or infirm dependants faced by today’s sandwich generation. but all this needs to be done in a smart way so that this does not suffer the same fate as the previous, or still current, proposal. that is why i intend to look, together with my colleagues vice-presidents timmermans and dombrovskis, as well as with commissioner thyssen, more broadly at the eu regulatory and policy framework and how it can be improved, given the real needs of parents and businesses in our changing world, and to propose up-to-date solutions to meet these needs. the commission will stay in close contact with parliament in order to reflect together all aspects that should be taken into account. we will also carry out a public consultation and will consult the social partners in accordance with their specific role in the field of social policy as laid down in the treaty. we will consider the full range of possible actions, both legislative and non-legislative measures, in order to have the most effective impact. i look forward to hearing members’ views and i count on their support.
blue-card question.– as you were the shadow rapporteur, do you not think that it is time for the council to engage in dialogue and start negotiations with parliament on the maternity leave directive, taking responsibility for refusing improvements in the safety and health at work of pregnant workers and workers who have recently given birth or are breastfeeding?

mr president, i am in favour of the adoption of the fourth eu anti—money laundering directive. as criminal and terrorist networks constantly evolve their tactics and methods, we must also adapt to the new threats posed by them. it was high time to address – and even to go beyond – the recommendations issued by the financial action task force in 2012 to tackle money laundering and terrorist financing and to have a european legal protection framework built around the highest international standards. the misuse of the financial system to channel illicit money or to finance terrorist activities threatens the good functioning, reputation and stability of the whole international financial system. this is why we needed the current europe-wide response to address such risks.
in writing. ‒ the eu has shown over time that it is concerned about the initiation and implementation of measures to combat money laundering derived from criminal offences. but these efforts have proved inadequate in the face of the increasingly common terrorist acts that shake our society. the use of the financial system to finance terrorism, such as taking hostages, forging administrative documents and running a terrorist group, are realities of contemporary society that need to be tackled with the utmost urgency by european and international forces. the use of the financial system for money laundering and terrorist financing causes serious damage to the stability of the european financial sector on a daily basis. however, through sustained efforts to increase the vigilance of banks, other financial actors, and by implication the client base as a whole, substantial contributions will be made to stopping these types of crime and to establishing a faster process for examining suspicious transactions. i voted in favour of the report because taking further measures to prevent the use of the financial system for money laundering and terrorist financing strengthens stability and transparency, thus helping to protect and encourage the legal economy.
in writing. ‒ i welcome the inclusion in this report of our group’s perspective regarding the setting up of a public register on beneficial owners. access to the public register on beneficial ownership is subject to a ‘legitimate interest’: this formulation will allow those member states which wish to be more transparent to adopt a broad definition of legitimate interest. member states may provide for an exemption to access to all or part of the beneficial ownership information on a case-by-case basis in exceptional circumstances, if this would expose a beneficial owner to the risk of fraud, kidnapping, blackmail, violence or intimidation or if the beneficial owner is a minor or otherwise incapable. the fourth anti-money-laundering directive will provide a sound basis for providing maximum transparency in respect of beneficial ownership of corporate structures across the eu.
in writing. ‒ i voted for the recommendation for second reading on the council's position at first reading with a view to adopting a directive of the european parliament and of the council on the prevention of the use of the financial system for the purpose of money laundering and terrorist financing, amending regulation (eu) no 648/2012 of the european parliament and of the council and repealing directive 2005/60/ec of the european parliament and of the council and commission directive 2006/70/ec. this project allows, among other things, greater control over the financial activity of publicly exposed persons, the interconnection of the taxation system of companies or the creation of transparency registers.
in writing. ‒ i supported this report in my vote today because it endorses the council's position on stopping the use of the financial system for money laundering and terrorist financing. money laundering is a major problem in all economies of the world, and the eu is no exception. unfortunately, in addition to the damage it does to economies, money laundering is used to fund a wide range of illegal and cross-border activities, such as drug trafficking, human trafficking, and, not least, terrorism. it is very clear that the sources of funding for terrorism globally are very diverse and it is equally clear that all the financial resources required for it go through a money laundering process at some point. to this end, it is necessary to set limits on the amounts that can be used to make cash payments, a method that is very difficult for the authorities to follow.
in writing. ‒ coordinated action by member states in the field of electronic bank transfers contributes to combating fraud and actions that can have serious repercussions on the security and credibility of the union's financial sector. first, financial institutions and payment service providers should ensure that they have all factual information on the originator and beneficiary of transactions and that the data recording requirements are in line with the fatf standards. cryptocurrencies and the payment methods used to make payments have led to the emergence of new illicit activities online. it's concerning that since 2008, when the new payment methods were made public, there have been reports of illegal activities aimed at money laundering, child pornography, drug trafficking, electronic fraud, identity theft using cryptocurrencies. therefore, authorising payment through virtual currencies should be allowed only if there is clear information about the persons involved and the subject matter of the transaction. in order to prevent transfers of funds for the purpose of fraudulent money laundering and terrorist financing, it is necessary to establish principles of cooperation with the authorities of third countries, to allow mutual access to complete information and to follow up on suspicious transactions.
in writing. ‒ this regulation lays down rules for payment service providers to send information on the payer and the payee throughout the payment chain for the purposes of prevention, investigation and detection of money laundering and terrorist financing. a coordinated response from law enforcement bodies in the ms and a standardised procedure for financial institutions and payment service providers is essential to combat money-laundering, which costs many billions annually. the main points of interest of the first reading negotiations concern transfers outside the union, where all information should be recorded, with the exception of a de minimis eur 1000 threshold, which should make remittances slightly easier. furthermore, the chapter on sanctions and monitoring has been enforced, and the provisions on data protection have been better aligned within the regulation.
in writing. ‒ i voted for the recommendation for second reading on the council's first reading position with a view to adopting a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on information accompanying transfers of funds and repealing regulation (ec) no 1781/2006. this document strengthens transparency and control over the origin of funds and financial transfers.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because it supports the document negotiated with the council, which brings a number of regulations on the information to be provided and collected when it comes to transfers of funds. the purpose of these regulations is not to make the work and bureaucracy for those involved in the transfer of funds more difficult, but to ensure a certain traceability of these funds in order to stop the financing of illegal activities and terrorist activities.
in writing. ‒ in a context where crossborder insolvency proceedings are no longer an exception but a current phenomenon affecting not only large enterprises or groups of enterprises but also smes, this commission proposal is welcome as an important initiative concerning european union company law. it is noted that there are certain areas of insolvency law where harmonisation is desirable and feasible, which is fully applicable at present. moreover, it should not be overlooked that disparities between national insolvency laws lead to competitive advantages or disadvantages and difficulties for undertakings with cross-border activities and could become obstacles to the successful restructuring of insolvent undertakings. i voted in favour of the report because i believe that a smooth, coordinated conduct of insolvency proceedings can play an important role in avoiding the winding up of groups and can contribute to a better appreciation of assets and the preservation of jobs.
in writing. ‒ i welcome the council regulation establishing a european framework for cross-border insolvency proceedings. this would determine which member state has jurisdiction for opening insolvency proceedings and establish uniform rules on applicable law, and provides for recognition and enforcing of insolvency-related decisions as well as for the coordination of main and secondary insolvency. our s&d group amendment managed to avert forum shopping by introducing the additional criteria of a three months cool—off period. the regulation now also allows for the coordination of the proceeding for corporate groups, and calls for a future introduction of preferential rights of employees. i thank the rapporteur and the shadows for the very good job done.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report because i believe that the rules on insolvency proceedings must be clear. as the text that this report supports shows, a number of eu-wide procedures are needed for insolvency, especially when we talk about the free market. in this context, the old regulations have been amended and modified to keep pace with the newest contexts, which leads to their ambiguities and misinterpretations. in these circumstances, the text adopted today, which brings all these changes into line and improves on the old procedures, was necessary to create clarity and predictability in the legislation.
in writing. ‒ the financial crisis that hit developed countries' economic sectors hard exposed the vulnerability of financial mechanisms and brought mineral resources back into focus as a potential factor for development. whether it's precious metals or rare earths and metals, which are essential to the technological process, they spark heated debate and lead to conflict. the recent technological advance and the horizontal expansion of the use of technology has, by default, led to an increase in the demand for mineral resources. there are very large interests behind the companies involved in mining, and the vulnerability of the authorities in resource-rich areas creates the conditions for escalating conflicts and flagrant violations of human rights. perhaps it should not be overlooked that whereas in the past communication channels were limited, today we are facing a new phenomenon due to the increasingly widespread access to the virtual environment, which, through the speed and avalanche of information, significantly contributes to the intensification and perpetuation of conflicts. i believe that we need a regulated and transparent framework for responsible sourcing of minerals in the eu, which ensures both traceability of minerals and that financial resources are not targeted at destinations with a risk factor in escalating conflicts.
in writing. ‒ i believe voluntary provisions, concerning only a simple link on the supply chain, are not enough to prevent the spread of conflicts. mandatory transparency requirements for the entire chain would make the real difference.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report proposed by the committee on international trade because it deals with an issue that i also discussed in my previous term of office, when i was on the committee on women's rights and gender equality, namely the control of mining in conflict zones. the money that comes from mining and trading minerals from conflict zones raises a problem that affects us indirectly. in many of these cases, we have clear situations of exploitation of people, impoverishment of the population and, not least, financial support for terrorist groups, paramilitaries and local mafias. it is essential that we have clearer control of the source of minerals and thus ensure that we do not end up sponsoring a modern form of slavery, paramilitary troops or even terrorist groups.
in writing. i voted for a voluntary supply chain certification scheme for importers of tin, tantalum and tungsten, their ores and gold - 3tg from conflict and high risk areas. i believe that we need an integrated eu approach to these areas and the report on conflict minerals was a proposal that also involves the accountability of all actors involved in this sector and is an important pillar of the integrated eu response. we need to build european capacity in these areas, we need to educate and empower all actors involved, including eu industry, but also governments of states facing local armed conflicts.
in writing. ‒ this directive aims to improve the environmental performance of products at all stages of their life cycle. some materials used in electronic products may lead to environmental and health hazards during their production or at the end of their life cycle. for these reasons, the eu has restricted the use of these materials. the elimination of cadmium is an essential factor in achieving these objectives and the delegated directive seeks to remove the ban on the use of cadmium in lighting and illumination applications of display systems. arguments such as the technical unavailability of cadmium-free quantum dots, given that there is a wide range of tvs based on this technology on the eu market, although the energy-saving properties of cadmium-free quantum dots are similar to those of cadmium, are not sufficiently convincing. i voted in favour of this motion for a resolution because such a derogation can only be dealt with in the context of a prior assessment, which has not yet been carried out.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of objecting to commission delegated directive of 30 january 2015 amending, for the purposes of adapting to technical progress, annex iii to directive 2011/65/eu of the european parliament and of the council as regards an exemption for cadmium in illumination and display lighting applications, considering the fact that rejection of the delegated directive therefore does not ban cadmium quantum dots, but only triggers a new assessment and that therefore there will be no market distortions, as the current exemption stays valid until revocation, with an additional grace period to be granted thereafter.

in writing. ‒ today we voted for mothers in the european union to have a guaranteed maternity leave. the european commission has to come up with a new proposal for a directive on maternity leave if it has to withdraw the current proposal, but i hope that the european executive will eventually succeed in reconciling the positions of parliament and the council in favour of mothers. it is not fair that the eu should give up on protecting the rights of pregnant women, especially as a number of women give up their professional plans to have children. europe's population is ageing and we need to ensure that the right conditions are in place to maintain demographic balance. i think that 20 weeks of fully paid maternity leave is not an absurd demand and i hope that member states will make it happen.
in writing. ‒ equality of opportunity is a sine qua non principle of european society. there is no doubt that protecting the rights of mothers and encouraging births are priorities to be pursued in all public policies at european and, by implication, national level. interinstitutional deadlock cannot stand in the way of common sense, natural principles which provide clear rules for the protection of mothers in europe and at the same time provide for equal opportunities between women and men, including in the matter of child rearing. we cannot be discouraged by the council's attitude when we know that women in europe are paid less than men for work of equal value and ignore the cold statistic that they too have pensions 39% lower. it is time to act and it is time for the european council to make the commitments it has to european citizens, commitments which include ensuring the protection of mothers and their rights to maternity leave, either by amending existing directives or by initiating new legislation.
in writing. ‒ whether we are talking about social integration or economic inclusion, people with disabilities need ongoing support. instruments such as the un convention on the rights of persons with disabilities at international level or the europe 2020 strategy for persons with disabilities at european level provide a concrete and comprehensive framework governing the situation of respect for the fundamental rights of persons with disabilities. in the context of economic and social integration, it is important to highlight that some 80 million people are often unable to participate fully in social and economic life because of physical and behavioural barriers. people with disabilities are more likely to be socially and economically excluded, so an integrated approach is needed to ensure that they enjoy the same rights. i voted in favour of this motion for a resolution because we must be aware that every citizen matters and that the problems of inclusion of people with disabilities are a barometer for the respect of human rights in society.

in writing. ‒ i have supported this report on the rights of persons with disabilities with my vote today. people with disabilities have great difficulty in finding jobs and in achieving equal rights, and unfortunately they are a very vulnerable group in our societies. there is an urgent need for very close cooperation and collaboration at eu level between the european parliament, the council and the commission. however, it is regrettable that in this case the importance of the european parliament was not respected, thus depriving the debate of the input of the citizens. i think that this report highlights many of the problems faced by disabled people without attempting to list them exhaustively. in this respect, i have supported and continue to support this position which seeks to bring citizens' direct participation in the decisions taken on this issue back into the debate.

in writing. ‒ the spread of xylella fastidiosa, which has now affected olive crops in northern italy but is likely to spread to vines, peaches, citrus and ornamental plants in the future, raises a serious alarm about the measures needed to stop its spread and prevent its spread. unfortunately, there is currently no treatment for infected plants and a significant number of wild plants carrying the bacteria do not show visible symptoms, which makes it difficult to identify and stop the spread of the bacterium. in order to prevent the emergence of new outbreaks, they consider that imports from areas where the bacterium has been identified should be prohibited and strict control and monitoring measures should be imposed on plants from suspected areas. i co-signed the resolution on the spread of xylella fastidiosa because i am convinced that we must react firmly and make every effort to create a quarantine procedure to stop the spread of the disease, as its effects can be disastrous for the entire european agricultural sector.
in writing. ‒ the phytosanitary emergency affecting olive groves in southern europe, especially in the apulia region of southern italy, potentially threatening other crops and regions, has assumed unprecedented and serious proportions, with dramatic economic, environmental and social consequences. on 28 april the standing committee for plant health of the european commission adopted a new decision aiming to stop the disease spreading to other regions. also imports of plants from regions known to be susceptible will be subject to strict conditions. member state experts also backed a ban on imports of coffee plants from honduras and costa rica due to the risk from the pest. as a result france has since lifted its ban on plant imports from areas hit by the bacteria in light of the reinforced eu action.

madam president, the eastern partnership is marked by something strange because before the vilnius summit in november 2013, there was already talk of the failure of that summit. we may have the same attitude now, a few hours before the opening, because some people are talking about failure. but, in the end - and we now know this - the vilnius summit was not a failure, if we take account, as some colleagues have already said, of the results that can be drawn since 2013. the signing of the association agreements, the progress made in facilitating visas and a whole series of other developments were mentioned. we are all aware that the societies to which the eastern partnership policy applies are not only looking for an assessment of the recent past but also for a promise, a message, a commitment for the future. i think that's our strength. i think we need to talk about the future. we must define a political ideal and a political commitment of europe to these eastern partnership countries. otherwise, with our pessimism and self-stigmatisation, we will not be able to resist russian propaganda which has only one message and one definition of the eastern partnership, namely an enterprise against moscow. that's what they say. i think we need courage in the face of this. it takes the courage of commitment and it takes a very clear view of the european future of the eastern partnership countries. it would be a pity if we were more modest in our proposals today than we were two or four years ago in warsaw. here's what i'm going to do.
madam president, since the last summit on the eastern partnership in vilnius many things have changed with our eastern partners and in particular those that signed association agreements with the eu and which are confronted with dramatically increasing external pressure. in ukraine, in fact, this external pressure is a war, with no insignia and russian troops spending their ʽholidaysʼ in eastern ukraine in armoured vehicles. the eu is seen as, and should concretely represent for the eastern partnership countries, a reliable partner which stands by them, helps them in their effort for reforms but also acknowledges their progress when this has been made. low ambition in riga will mean a dramatic impact – a negative one – on europe and on our eastern side. i call on both sides, the commission and the member states, to make sure that the riga summit sends the positive message our eastern partners need. the eu cannot and must not suffocate the expectations and aspirations of our partners and their people, but must rather encourage and compensate their efforts, show them that the european integration path is even more open than before and offer them messages and opportunities that can also counter the heavy pressure from russian propaganda. from this point, i see a clear and important step that should be taken, namely the free visa regime for georgia and ukraine. let us not give something else, but something we can do and which should be done according to the efforts those countries have made. it is the first and the most important sign that their future lies with europe and we should continuously fight for this. finally, i unconditionally back, and i proudly join, the letter initiated by our colleague, mr auštrevičius.
madam president, as we speak history is being written and age-defining changes are under way. in the coming years, we should be able to look back to now with the conviction that we did the right thing and provided the right response to the critical challenges facing eastern europe. i will focus on the element of ambitions and membership perspective: we need to do more for those who have real and tangible european ambitions, for those who have decided on the european path. of course, much needs to be done, and words are less credible than concrete and tangible actions, but the eu should send a clear signal to moldova, georgia and ukraine that their future is with the 28 member states as long as they genuinely fulfil their obligations and show real commitment to the association agreements’ reform agenda. we cannot ask them to implement harsh reforms without having light at the end of the tunnel. if they deliver, they should be considered serious candidates on the road to the eu.
madam president, ms kalniņa-lukaševica said that we, the european union, are offering a genuine partnership to these three countries. unfortunately, we are offering less than expected. we are making a step back in comparison with the last eastern partnership in vilnius. these countries need a real european perspective. this is what they are looking for and, unfortunately, at this summit that is going to start tomorrow, we are transforming these three countries into kind of buffer states. it is a step back; like a concession offered to russia. also, i agree with the council in supporting the earliest possible ratification by all member states of the association agreements and the deep and comprehensive free trade area with georgia, moldova and ukraine. these agreements are fundamental in order to strengthen political association and economic integration.
in writing. promoting state-building and consolidating the rule of law for partner countries is an important area of multilateral cooperation in the eastern partnership. this is particularly important in the light of the situation in ukraine, where it is in all our interests, in addition to upholding our security policy objectives, to see ukraine emerge from the crisis stronger. it is not only necessary for the economic renewal of the country, but also for the stability of the institutional system, the reduction of corruption and the genuine application of the rule of law. in this context and as time goes on, we must speak more and more often about the part of the minsk agreement that deals with constitutional reform, decentralisation and the guarantee of the rights of national minorities. i think that these issues cannot be avoided at the eastern partnership summit.
madam president, the eu-celac summit is fundamental in order to strengthen relations between european, latin-american and caribbean countries. this will be a useful platform to discuss regional and global issues with our partners. hopefully this year we will have the chance to talk about eu-cuba relations, about the venezuela situation and about the colombian peace process, as well as about the trade agreement with mexico and the revitalisation of trade agreements with mercosur. i completely agree with ms mogherini when she states that we share cultural and historical roots and a wish for peace and prosperity. i would also like to underline the importance of the eurolat parliamentary assembly to strengthening the monitoring of democracy and legitimisation as part of cooperation between countries.
madam president, i would like to start by welcoming the decision to supplement the pre-financing of the youth employment initiative. for maximum impact, i encourage the commission to devote even more resources to programmes aimed at combating unemployment, with a focus on encouraging entrepreneurship among young people and women, and to work together with the member states, the european investment fund, the european investment bank to set up an advisory group to develop financing mechanisms for new businesses by young people and women in each member state. this will facilitate their development. this is the only way to keep their creative ideas in the european union. as for the education system, in my opinion, it should be grounded in reality and as practical as possible. to achieve this, we must urge member states to improve and intensify relations between the main actors involved, namely governments, employers, public or private educational institutions and, not least, civil society organisations in each member state. as a youth representative, i believe that schools should offer graduates a real start and ensure that they make a smooth transition into the workplace.
madam president, seven million unemployed young people, seven million people whose future is in question - a project like the youth employment initiative should have created new jobs, especially in the disadvantaged areas. in contrast, projects are missing, even though the pre-financing rate for them has increased. we can no longer afford to wait for the member states to wake up. therefore, if the states are not able, i propose that these funds be transformed into programmes managed directly by the european union and into grants and de minimis aid for young people, schools or the employing company. we need to realise that unemployed young people can no longer wait for national bureaucracies to move and need measures that are easy to understand, use and access. every day that passes is more than a procedural step and a day in the lives of seven million young europeans who have lost hope of living a normal life. because some of the member states don't care!
in writing. both as a romanian mep and as a representative of the romanian social democratic youth, i know that young europeans have remained in a period of crisis. while europe has largely overcome the period of unjustified austerity and the economic and financial crisis, young europeans are today in an identity crisis. unemployment, although starting to decline in some member states, is still high enough to raise serious questions about the future of europe. the european youth initiative, built on the european youth guarantee, a programme proposed by s&d and pes, needs shock measures to deliver better results. the emergency funding of measures to assist young people in member states where unemployment among young people is high is very important. we want to have the tools to offer every young european a job, a training programme, an internship or an apprenticeship within four months of completing their last form of education or becoming unemployed. if we want to put the accelerator on, we should do it now, through pre-financing funds allocated by the commission under the european youth initiative.
madam president, the matter of whaling activities in japan is absolutely not of subsidiary importance and cannot be left out in our talks with japan. our reason is that the protection of biodiversity and of the environment is at the core of our european principles and values and, if we do not want to be called irresponsible, incoherent and weak, we must always take this into consideration in our relationship with other countries. this is a matter of having the holistic ambitious and far-sighted view that we owe to european citizens and to the entire world population. moreover, i believe we must think twice before skipping talks on important matters and before engaging with a partner that does not respect international law. japan must comply with the spirit and the letter of the international court of justice ruling and refrain from further whaling activities in the antarctic until such time as the international whaling commission gives a contrary opinion – all the more so given our shared interest in the rules—based international order and effective multilateralism. i do not understand nor support the exclusion of an environmental interest in our talks with japan. we should honestly represent our citizens’ concerns, make their voices heard and solve this issue once and for all. i therefore strongly invite vice—president mogherini to raise this issue at the upcoming eu-japan summit on 29 may.

member of the commission.– mr president, i would like to thank my dear colleague ms toia for her question and for her contribution. i am here just to deliver the following statement on behalf of commissioner miguel arias cañete who unfortunately cannot be here today. the commission shares the view of the european parliament that acer will play a key role in the compilation and proper functioning of the internal energy market (iem). the implementation by acer of the remit which ensures the effective monitoring of the wholesale energy market is essential for the functioning of the iem. the commission is committed to ensuring that the agency is adequately equipped to perform all its relevant tasks. it has so far ensured that the level of funding allocated to the agency is sufficient and will be vigilant and propose additional funding when these prove necessary. when carrying out its assessment, the commission will also consider the energy union framework strategy adopted in february this year, 2015, which has further emphasised acer’s role in completing the eu’s internal energy market.
blue-card question. – madam president, there is something i would like to understand, because it seems that for mr kariņš the issue is only the number of staff of acer. is it possible to speak only about the number of staff when talking about the task to detect and deter market abuse? is that the only issue?
madam president, if we really want to achieve a european energy union we need to fully liberalise the 28 national energy markets, to ensure the integration of these markets by achieving their physical interconnection, but we also need to harmonise national regulations and monitor these markets. we therefore need to strengthen the work of this european agency, both in terms of coordinating the work of national agencies and in terms of monitoring energy markets. we cannot accept negative practices such as those which assign additional tasks to the agency without also allocating the necessary resources. they de-motivate staff and dilute responsibility.
madam president, energy security must be a permanent concern for the european union and the member states. this requires close cooperation between countries to enable them to identify common, cross-border solutions, thus giving them the opportunity to rapidly develop their own energy resources. we are in a period where we are faced with threats and constraints due to energy dependence, and some member states are being forced to make a series of compromises to meet their domestic energy needs, but at very high costs. the regulatory measures imposed by remit on the wholesale energy market must ensure the security of the information transmitted and remove any suspicion of market manipulation. that is why we believe that acer must be strong enough - and here we emphasise: well-sized - to have the capacity to cooperate effectively with the national authorities and the competent financial authorities. this will enable the exchange of information between the two parties, enabling the commission to monitor transactions, assess and identify abuses with a view to remedying them.
madam president, i believe that the european union agency for the cooperation of energy regulators (acer) has a key role for the transparency of the wholesale energy market. acer estimates it needs another 45 full—time staff to effectively monitor energy transactions and thus prevent fraud and market manipulation, which has a negative effect on energy prices and consumer trust. considering that the commission has so far only allocated 15 new staff members, i agree that, in order to effectively carry out an important task such as detecting and deterring market abuse, the commission should allocate sufficient resources.
mr president, state-sponsored violence in zimbabwe has reduced since more than 200 people were killed during the disputed 2008 elections. i am wondering how many people must be killed before state-sponsored violence in zimbabwe disappears once and for all. the forced disappearance of civil society activist itai dzamara echoes the darkest days of zimbabwe’s political instability. it is only the latest of events that show how in zimbabwe a worsening of human rights and democracy is taking place, as well as harassment and abuses against human rights defenders, journalists and members of civil society. i stand by the 83 courageous civil society organisations that called for the immediate release of itai dzamara, otherwise demanding the resignation of president robert mugabe. finally, i call on the responsible authorities to stop ignoring the high court and to comply with this ruling, taking all the necessary measures to find mr itai dzamara and bring all those responsible to justice. blue-card answer.– on many occasions in the committee on development i have maintained that the european union has to use the leverage of humanitarian aid and of development aid for all these african countries, and other countries, led by dictators, where they do not respect human rights, they do not respect the law – they respect nothing. we should, indeed, use all necessary leverage to put all such countries on the right path to respecting international law and the law in general.
on behalf of the ppe group.– mr president, as is the case with the migrant crisis in the mediterranean, we can state that the exodus by boat of myanmar’s muslim residents is not a new phenomenon. in 2009, for example, many rohingya refugees were rescued after 21 days at sea. similar root causes behind this mass movement of people can also be distinguished, namely poverty, violence and persecution. here as well, the most vulnerable groups are victims of human trafficking, of which the recent discovery of mass graves in thailand is a gruesome testimony. the last parallel is the potential loss of credibility, not only for the asean countries involved who are benefiting from the gcp scheme, but also for the eu if it decides to ignore these violations of international human rights law. the european external action service should put pressure on myanmar to grant genuine citizenship to the rohingya and should encourage all countries concerned to develop a solid cooperation scheme that aims at tackling the human trafficking networks.
mr president, the discovery of mass graves in thailand and the appalling situation of the rohingya refugees adrift in south-east asia are a humanitarian disaster. thousands of migrants are still reported to be trapped by smugglers for weeks. we cannot help drawing parallels here with the refugee crisis we are facing in the mediterranean. whether in south asia or the mediterranean, the only possible solution is a regional one. we must therefore encourage all the countries of the region to take part in the bangkok conference next week in an attempt to achieve an integrated solidarity mechanism. we must not turn the ball over and disengage from the problem as burma is unfortunately doing. the agreement reached yesterday between malaysia, indonesia and thailand, which provides for humanitarian assistance and the temporary reception of migrants, is a positive development, but the lasting solution obviously requires granting civil rights to the rohingya, who are persecuted in burma. i would add a word because i proposed not to move the debate on the urgent debate to the morning on the grounds that there are more people in the afternoon. we have proof of this today, as we are fewer than in the afternoon. we must return to the debate on emergencies in the afternoon.
mr president, we all know that rohingya are one of the most persecuted populations in the world. they continue to be smuggled through thailand and from other countries in the region by human traffickers and held captive in inhuman conditions in jungle camps in the south of thailand, where they are tortured, starved and beaten to death. we must cooperate with these countries to put an end to these atrocities and to this extremely serious violation of human rights. i strongly encourage myanmar to grant full citizenship to its rohingya minority and grant them equal access to services. moreover, i find it unacceptable that refugees are pushed back into the sea. this is a violation of international law and human rights law and we should take it into consideration in the next talks with thailand, indonesia and malaysia.
mr president, i believe it is very important that international solidarity is expressed to the political opponents who have been imprisoned by swaziland’s monstrous royal decree. we cannot turn a blind eye to the conditions of political prisoners. this is a matter of human dignity and social justice. swaziland engaged itself, under the cotonou agreement, to respect democracy, the rule of law and human rights principles, which include freedom of expression and freedom of the media. the government should stand by the promises it made, take concrete measures to respect and promote freedom of expression, guarantee democracy and plurality, and establish a legislative framework allowing the full participation of political parties in line with international and regional human rights obligations. the authorities of swaziland should guarantee, in all circumstances, the physical and psychological integrity of swazi political and civil rights prisoners and release them without delay.
in writing. ‒ the common security and defence policy emerged and developed as a natural consequence of the process of european integration, as the benefits of joint action under the union's aegis became apparent at international level. it is essentially the sum of decisions taken jointly by the member states concerning their relations through the union with the other actors in the international system. the european security environment, especially in the eastern and southern neighbourhood of the european union, is increasingly unstable and volatile due to the number of challenges. a number of conflicts, such as those in eastern ukraine, syria and iraq, the rise of the terrorist organisation isis, the crisis in libya or the terrorist threat in africa, pose direct threats to the security of the european union. i voted in favour of this report because the common security and defence policy provides a framework for cooperation within which the european union can carry out operational missions in third countries, the main objective of these missions being to maintain peace and strengthen international security.
in writing. ‒ the report has a particular importance in view of the preparations for the june 2015 council meeting on the common security and defence policy – a meeting that should sum up the efforts made in the last one and a half years (since the previous december 2013 meeting) aimed at making the csdp more efficient. the text is aimed at tackling a few aspects of interest: an assessment of the overall security context to clarify if the csdp has become a real priority; to evaluate the situation in the csdp missions and operations; and to assess the situation of the capabilities and of the eu defence industry.
in writing. – with the new appointment of federica mogherini as the new vice-president of the commission and high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy, interest in the csdp has risen and most likely will be reflected by a development boost of the csdp. i have voted for this report because it will implement a more pronounced stance towards conflict prevention at european union level.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this text as i support the overall line it draws, despite the fact that in my own view we should be doing much more in the wake of the ukrainian crisis. the report does note accurately some main issues and i believe our efforts in the eu should go towards solving these problems: we need to have real political will to contribute troops and money to eu strategic efforts; we need to use what we have, such as the battlegroups; we need to act more in actual strategic ways, involving ourselves more in areas where we can make a real difference rather than being there when the crisis is over. and finally, the official language needs to stop being so self-congratulatory for minimalistic efforts, like low-scale training missions, when there are so many security crises worldwide with a direct impact on the prosperity and security of europe.
in writing. ‒ at a time when we are increasingly faced with various external threats, the european union's security and defence policy requires a reassessment in order to strengthen our crisis intervention and response capabilities. the most recent example, the mediterranean migrant crisis, highlights limited capacity and the lack of coordinated action by member states. operation triton, in which no less than 20 member states participated, has exposed the shortcomings of the union in the area of the security of the external borders. in order to address the terrorist threats, which have become more frequent in recent times, concrete measures are required to increase the effectiveness, visibility and impact of the csdp. new threats such as cyber-attacks, border vulnerabilities and communication security need to be considered. strengthening planning and rapid response capacity for coordinated mission delivery is achieved through more comprehensive defence investment and more effective management of existing assets. member states should also endeavour to develop the european defence industry by enhancing civil and military research collaboration.
in writing. ‒ the eu has to assume its role at global level not only from the economic and political point of view, but as well from the security point of view. that comes particularly at a moment when the level of security challenges for eu have increased and, consequently, strengthening the csdp is more than ever a must. a new method is necessary to be adopted as regards the financing of the csdp missions and operations in order to increase their efficiency. the priority stays in developing a financial mechanism for the deployment of the eu civilian missions and military operations in a faster and more flexible way, while having the full logistical and financial support in order to fulfil the objectives they are entrusted with. that is why, among others, we need to alleviate today’s very bureaucratic system of procurement. the permanent csdp warehouse should quickly be upgraded by enlarging its scope and by improving the availability of stored equipment, and enlarge, as well, the diversity of it.
in writing. – the idea of a common defence policy for europe dates back to 1948 when the uk, france, and the benelux signed the treaty of brussels. csdp was on the agenda of the december 2013 european council meeting when the heads of states discussed how to enhance defence capabilities, strengthen the defence industry and improve the effectiveness, visibility and impact of the csdp. now, this report will bring new concrete measures, pragmatic solutions, cost savings/efficiency-increasing initiatives, transparency and accountability. as shadow rapporteur, i have voted for this report calling for a strengthened cooperation mechanism between member states.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this very important budgetary text due to the need we have in the european union for member states to start listening to the recommendations found within. we have, collectively, one of the worldʼs largest defence expenditure budgets, yet individually our member states are badly underfinanced in terms of the helsinki headline goals. we have significant potential and we are wasting it by refusing to cooperate, by having joint programmes only in the least sensitive areas and by allowing nationalistic, limited mindsets to prevail in our defence ministries. the european union needs to start planning and spending money in a comprehensively complementary way. we need to stop duplication or even investing in obsolete capacities and to start using our financial resources, which are quite ample if we look at the total figure, in a realistic way.
in writing. ‒ defence policy is one of the european union's most important instruments in an international and regional context marked by increased instability and a high level of threats to the national security of many of the european union's members. i welcome the call for a stronger dimension to the common security and defence policy the objectives of this policy are unattainable if the resources available are not adequate. i also believe that there is a need for increased cooperation between the civil and military spheres. the instrumental nature of the common security and defence policy is best served by close cooperation between the two levels. it is also important that the actions taken under this policy correspond to the current security concerns of the member states. a faster and more flexible approach is beneficial. however, this change is essentially dependent on the allocation of additional financial resources and i support in this context the extension of the eligible costs under the athena mechanism.
in writing. ‒ in an environment characterised by a significant increase in the number of armed conflicts, low-intensity crises, hybrid or intermediate war, failed states or frequent human rights violations in the immediate neighbourhood of the european union, but also by the threat of terrorism inside and outside the eu, an approach in a coordinated and unified manner at union level is necessary. particular attention should be paid to the impact of certain projects on the autonomy and independence of the european union, and member states should give priority to the military or defence industries and provide incentives for their development, to the extent that european union legislation allows. i voted in favour of this report because i believe that the success of csdp peacekeeping and security missions depends on the achievement of a european defence market to eliminate overlaps and reduce red tape.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report since it aims at building an innovative and competitive european industry and making the best possible use of the security and defence budget. i agree on the idea that the commission and the member states must take defence procurement into account when negotiating international trade agreements. moreover, i support the idea that the commission should step up its efforts to achieve a level playing field in european defence markets in order to fight protectionist practices by member states by promoting cross-border cooperation and better access to defence industry supply chains.
in writing. ‒ i voted for this report concerning the impact of developments in european defence markets on the security and defence capabilities in europe (2015/2037((ini)). recent events in europe show an increasing need to strengthen the defence potential of all 28 member states. security is an issue which concerns us all and this is why security threats need to be addressed in a transparent and coordinated fashion. defence spending at eu level is eur 190 billion – an enormous amount of money. the defence budgets are being spent in a very inefficient way due to delays and incoordination. this money is tax payers’ money. not having a common defence market implies the risk of corruption in public procurement. this is why i support a common security defence framework in order to enable the union to deal efficiently with security threats, ensure eu competition and at the same time to protect the money of the citizens.
in writing. – taking into consideration the current political threats at the eu’s eastern borders, the alarming decrease of development in the defence market due to budget cuts, and growing external dependencies, i have voted for this report in order to re—establish european autonomy through increased cooperation and co—ordination between member states.
in writing. ‒ i voted for ms gomesʼ report as it highlights the very real risk of fragmentation in the european defence market at a point where we might need it more than in the past 20 years. with rising violent extremism, failed states, instability in our neighbourhood and armed aggression against our partner countries, we cannot afford that each member state decides unilaterally to cut defence budgets, abandon defence research and development or, perhaps even worse, duplicate the capabilities of other member states which they could share together, saving a great deal of money. we cannot afford either for many states to keep buying or reconditioning obsolete technologies from outside the european markets, and i believe the 2009 defence package should be a main priority for implementation in all the member states which have not yet done so.
mr president, i will also add my voice and ask the conference of presidents to consider the possibility of declaring a conflict of interests to be present when any politician or political party in this house gets loans from abroad. this is the case with the front national and i will ask personally the conference of presidents to consider this very seriously.
madam president, the rise of the terrorist threat must cause the g7 summit to have as its main agenda the tightening of the rules against the financing of terrorism at the international level. to this end, an effective analysis of the tracking and combating of payment methods and instruments targeting terrorist groups is needed. we see today that fundamentalist militants of the islamic state are providing substantial revenues to finance their military campaigns in syria and iraq, from trading in various forms of oil and natural gas from isis-controlled territories. this requires urgent and firm measures to ban these transactions, considering that blocking the accounts of those cooperating with islamic militants is a necessary solution to eradicate these actions. unfortunately, some eu states are unable to effectively protect their borders, opening doors for waves of migrants, creating vulnerabilities for the entire eu, given that the masks of migrants can be hidden by islamic state fighters. furthermore, we note that in the neighbourhood of the european union, more precisely in the republic of moldova, suspected persons with links to the islamic state have been identified. cryptocurrencies are another vulnerability that terrorist groups exploit. all these aspects should lead to the g7 summit focusing on what it means for all states to join forces to strengthen security in order to combat terrorist groups effectively.
in writing.– i believe it is of the utmost importance that, at the next g7 summit, world leaders will discuss how to achieve sustainable growth in the face of record debt levels, as well as how to regulate the financial markets and how to improve cooperation on international tax policy. i hope that the g7 ministers will follow up on their commitment to reach a deal on climate change that is ambitious, robust and inclusive, in order to be effective in limiting the increase in global temperature to 20c above the pre-industrial level.
in writing.– this summit takes place against a background of increasing geopolitical tensions, and it should tackle the pressing issues of our time. i consider that there are some priorities which should be addressed at the forthcoming summit besides foreign and security policy and sustainable economic growth. of course, the g7 should work to ensure peace and security: the ongoing conflict in ukraine and the threat posed by isis should be at the top of the agenda. the implementation of the minsk agreement should be evaluated, and we must tighten checks on suspected terrorist financing. however, infrastructure modernisation and development research should also be on the agenda, and we should not forget the struggle against tax fraud and tax avoidance. the initial expectations are high and we need to see concrete results.
mr president, i congratulate marc tarabella on his work on this report. i believe that the current structure of the two programmes leads to an efficient reinforcement of the educational dimension of young people to know food and its source, to increase the consumption of selected agricultural products and to train healthy eating, thus improving the perception of agriculture and its products. the mandatory educational measures proposed by the commission to accompany the distribution of fruit, vegetables and milk in schools are welcome and, like the rapporteur, i believe it is essential to promote a healthy and balanced diet from an early age, by re-teaching young people to know food and its origin, to become familiar with its taste and texture and to get closer to local producers. that's why i support this report, and if i were to summarize the reasons, they would be about health, education, support for fruit, vegetable and dairy farmers, but also support for local producers and local markets.
in writing. almost one third of european children are overweight or obese. that is why i would first of all like to underline the important educational role of the school fruit and vegetables scheme and hope for the best possible implementation in the member states. the creation of a common legal framework for the two programmes is welcome, especially in view of the situation in the dairy and fruit sectors, which are heavily affected by the russian embargo. i also welcome the commission's proposal on flexibility. it is essential that member states are able to transfer funds between programmes to respond to the challenges faced by indigenous sectors. but i would like to draw attention to the importance of using short supply chains in the distribution of milk and fruit in schools. it's crucial that students are connected to farmers and agricultural production. it is also important that the products are distributed as naturally as possible, without added sweeteners, and that the fruit is fresh and, if possible, locally grown and as naturally as possible, without pesticides and chemical fertilizers. i hope that there will be a rapid agreement between the institutions on this regulation and that the member states will successfully implement it.
mr president, european development aid must have the objective of reaching the ones most in need, and considering the situation in eritrea the eu delegation must closely monitor the use of this funding. it is clear that increasing political dialogue with the government about human rights on the basis of article 8 of the cotonou agreement is needed as well as an increase in direct support to the civil society and human rights defenders. it seems that the un commission of inquiry on human rights in eritrea has had no cooperation from the eritrean regime and that this commission has not been granted access to the country. these facts raise concerns about the decision to triple the aid given to eritrea. there seems to be no evidence of any real change in terms of human rights in eritrea. the european commission should halt its implementation of the aid package until the un commission of inquiry on eritrea has been given access to the country in order to assess the situation.

madam president, the attack on french tv channel tv5monde on wednesday, 8 april highlighted europe’s vulnerability to high—tech cyber criminality. i believe that these attacks signal a new level of threat to western media as well as civil and military networks, and we cannot find the eu unprepared. we must focus on securing key eu networks – transportation, energy, financial or healthcare networks. we must achieve cyber resilience as well as a common high level of security. i support options such as requirements for eu countries to provide national nis strategies and for the constitution of agencies to facilitate cross-border cooperation at eu level. i hope that soon i will hear from the commission and from the council about how they intend to implement cyber-security strategy.
in writing. cyberattacks against the media represent a new threat to cybersecurity, aimed at generating terror and threatening one of the fundamental institutions of democracy. these attacks demonstrate, once again, that no one is immune from danger and prove that today's terrorism and cybercrime can have devastating effects that directly affect citizens. the european commission and the member states need to adopt rapid solutions to improve cybersecurity at european level. this, in my view, requires better cooperation between national and european institutions, with a real link between efforts to combat such dangers together. i am pleased that my country, romania, is at the forefront of the fight against cyberattacks, through its highly qualified specialists and institutions, and i take this opportunity to suggest again to the european institutions the creation of a european cybersecurity body based in romania.
mr president, traditions, especially those of indigenous and minority groups, are essential as they often embody the continuous existence of a community. however, as we saw a couple of years ago, certain countries tried to push through a process to legitimise the concept of ‘traditional values of humankind’ as the basis for human rights law at the human rights council, led by the russian federation. there is an inherent danger to making ‘traditional values’ the standard for human rights. not only do these values evolve constantly, they are also difficult and dangerous to define. it is within this context that culture cannot be used to undermine the universality of the human rights principles, which are applicable to the practice of early and forced marriage of girls. firstly, the eu ensures that gender equality is on the agenda in every dialogue with third countries, especially for development cooperation. however, it should keep on mainstreaming gender equality in all policy areas and programmes, especially inside the union. too many girls in europe are still deprived of their right to education, because they are forced into marriage. secondly, there is an urgent need for reliable data on forced marriages inside the european union. lastly, parliament has urged the commission in the past to promote the national ratification of the istanbul convention and even launched the procedure for the eu’s accession to it. i urge commissioner jourová to pursue this as a priority so that the battle against forced and early marriages can take place in a harmonised way across the entire european union.
mr. president, according to united nations population fund statistics, 14.2 million young girls under the age of eighteen are or will be married each year between 2011 and 2020 in developing countries, mainly sub-saharan africa and south asia, which represents 39,000 forced marriages every day. the percentage is staggering, and the statistics don't stop there: one in four teenage girls is married against her will between the ages of fourteen and eighteen; one in nine young girls is married by force between the ages of ten and fourteen; one in two girls gives birth to a baby while still a teenager in developing countries. we should also not forget that in 2009 more than half of the world's population, or 50.6%, lived on less than 0.70 euros a day, which encourages forced marriages for young girls who are still seen as a source of income for their families. in fact, in these countries, girls and teenage girls are objects that their parents dispose of and sell to their future husbands. if we consider that about 36 percent of children over six have never been to school, and where schools exist, the average class size is 129 students, we understand that in these countries marriage is often a solution or perhaps the only possible solution to survive for young women without education. ..the president interrupted the speaker. ) the rapporteur agreed to answer a question raised after the blue card had been raised, in accordance with rule 162 (8) of the rules of procedure).

mr president, romania's entry into the schengen area is not only a necessity, but also an act of justice. the recent waves of migrants demonstrate that there are countries in the european union which, although they belong to the schengen area, have serious problems securing their borders, and the european authorities are obliged to take urgent measures in the spirit of human solidarity, which is also natural, by setting quotas of migrants for each country. it is unclear, however, why romania is denied access to the schengen area, even though its borders are very secure, meeting the technical conditions, being the provider of security in southeastern europe. we have obligations and we fulfill them, but we don't understand why our rights are not respected. and the romanians need firm answers. when will the principle of mutual solidarity apply to rights as well as obligations? i think romania's entry into the schengen area must be done immediately, otherwise those responsible will prove that the double language is at home here in europe and we do not want that.
