mr president, many are asking us why the economy of the united states has recovered easier, faster and in a more convincing way from the previous economic and financial crisis than our european economy. the answer to this rests partly with a quick restructuring of its banking sector and with a reform of its financial system, which of course has consequences on the financing of the economy, on growth and, subsequently, on jobs. the capital markets union, commissioner, represents one of the lessons that europe has learned from the crisis, and by implementing it now it will ensure better financing for our economy and our smes. i would, therefore, like to particularly stress the importance of one element of the question put to you: sme-friendly economic and regulatory conditions. i think the commission should indeed focus on ensuring the successful and diversified access of smes to financing in the capital markets union. every detail from your side regarding this initiative will be very much welcomed. however, national particularities of the business sector and business models of the financial sectors in different european countries must also be considered when providing equal opportunities for financing. the banking sector should remain an important source of financing and funding for smes in europe. therefore, a genuine european approach should take into consideration the interconnected character of the banking and financial sectors in europe and should be a support to the internal market in europe, also with the aim of avoiding financial fragmentation, especially in times of crisis.
blue-card question. – ms kyllönen, yes, it seems that we are going to see heaven on earth with the circular economy. this might be true, but do you not think that, first of all, we need innovation? without innovation, this circular economy is not going to function. first of all, we need innovation and a high—efficiency circular economy. only societies that are going to base their economies on innovation are going to win in the future.
mr. president, in 1900, the population of the planet was no more than two billion. by 2050, it will exceed 9 billion. the current rate of resource consumption is unsustainable. this consumption generates not only a negative impact on the environment, but also other effects, including political tensions that are increasingly difficult to manage. we easily waste food, even though malnutrition and hunger are choking entire regions of the world. we make geopolitical trade-offs for expensive energy, but we ignore the opportunity to use more renewable energy. we have access to fruit grown thousands of miles away in stores, but we don't always find it easily on the same shelves as fruit produced by local farmers. all of these are forms of waste. the transition to more responsible consumption is absolutely essential. the principle of a circular economy with a greater focus on reuse and recycling is a good one. it would remove the pressure on finite resources and create opportunities and jobs in the recycling industry.
mr president, europe is making efforts to integrate ecological and social risks into financial legislation, in order to channel capital as appropriately as possible towards appropriate services in the fields of ecosystems and biodiversity. i believe that environmental degradation, excessive use of resources and lack of appropriate measures can lead to undesirable long-term effects. on the other hand, greater attention needs to be paid to the efficient use of resources in construction and buildings, given that at european level buildings account for 40% of the total energy consumption of the european union, which generates 36% of total carbon dioxide emissions. europe needs sustainable buildings, but to do so we need smart and sustainable land-use planning, complemented by good land-use planning and adequate transport solutions.

in writing. the circular economy is good for both the economy and the environment. the initiative to have the european parliament's position on the content of a future draft european legislation prepared by the european commission stated in parliament is therefore welcome. there are wide differences between the member states of the union in the state of progress towards achieving a circular economy, in particular in the recovery and re-use of technological and household waste. that is why i argue that future european regulation should contain clear standards and targets for each member state.
madam president, commissioner, i would like to stress once again that over time it has become increasingly clear that milk prices and farmers' incomes have not been supported and stabilised sufficiently effectively. i agree with the rapporteur that the implementation of the measures introduced by the milk package is uneven in the member states and i am very concerned for small producers. for example, the elimination of quotas in romania is estimated to lead to the imminent disappearance of some 800 000 small local producers. i believe that the european union's policy on the production of milk by small producers should be supported to prevent it from being abandoned, and i would therefore like to recall some of the threats facing the sector: the closure of the market with russia, the invasion of certain markets by cheaper products from certain eu countries, unfair competition and food fraud in the agri-food chain and the milk supply chain, large social disparities in rural areas, the lack of alternation in rural employment. the european commission needs to strengthen the stabilisation of the retail market to regulate the taking of profits by small producers and support the strengthening of small producers' associations, particularly in eastern europe. i hope, commissioner, that you're considering this.
madam president, the dairy sector is one of the most vulnerable sectors in agriculture. i congratulate commissioner phil hogan on his work but at the same time i think that there needs to be a more energetic concern on the part of the commission so that the most effective means of protecting this sector are identified. the disappearance of milk quotas seriously and unacceptably exacerbates the imbalances between large farmers and small farmers, so that the existence of the latter is seriously endangered. the embargo imposed by russia on dairy products and beyond is likely to cause market shifts, generating imbalances even in countries that have not had direct trade relations with them. in some countries, such as romania, milk prices have reached 10 euro cents per litre, well below cost, and small farmers are on the verge of imminent bankruptcy. in view of the volatility of prices, the commission must immediately include in its work programme measures to strengthen and protect this sector at european level, and finding new markets such as the one offered by ttip, as well as developing existing ones, must be a major concern. mechanisms, including fiscal facilities, should also be put in place to encourage the establishment of producer associations and organisations capable of processing milk into finished products and further developing their own distribution chains to manage them. only then can we talk about security in the milk sector.
madam president, dairy farmers continue to be hard hit by the combination of the ending of the milk quota regime and the effects of the russian embargo. i congratulate my colleagues from the s&d group who put emphasis on the situation of the primary producers and particularly those operating on a smaller scale on family farms or from more remote areas. the risks of further concentration of milk production in more competitive areas is still a lurking threat for such farms, and the report now contains a set of proposals and demands which could form a minimum set of safeguards. i am confident that the s&d group agriculture committee members will remain in close contact, and if the situation deteriorates we will ring the alarm bells again in the future to ensure primary dairy production is safeguarded. finally, i believe it is important to strengthen the milk market observatory to give producers more timely access to accurate market information.
in writing. the current context on the milk market after the expiry of quotas requires special attention to be paid to milk producers, who are faced with a new reality. price volatility is an essential aspect to be taken into account in the light of experience to date and the increasing competition on the milk market. manufacturers should be able to foresee price margins in order to develop a market strategy adapted to the real market requirements. i consider that a review of the reference price for products subject to intervention is necessary in order to make the measures adopted so far by the commission more effective and attractive. i think the milk market observatory could be improved by equipping it with a set of indicators for better monitoring of the market. these indicators should provide information on price margins and include both the member state and regional dimension without increasing the administrative burden. however, this transparency should protect the interests of the various entities in the milk supply chain.
madam president, on 7 august 2015 it will be one year since russia imposed a ban on food imports from the countries of the european union. according to the analyses of financial institutions, at the end of the first year of the ban, the european union loses eur 6.7 billion and about 130 000 jobs. in this economic war, romania is hit twice. if the first effect was the loss of export contracts with russia in the milk processing industry, where production fell by a quarter compared to the pre-ban period, and the pork industry had to reduce prices by 25%, accumulating huge losses, romanian producers also had to cope with the influx of goods coming to the romanian market from european union countries, which were also subject to the same bans. in the context of a foreseeable decision by moscow to extend the embargo by at least one year, the european union must find a formula for supporting romanian producers as soon as possible. in the absence of this support, the forecasts are downright alarming and go as far as the total bankruptcy of the two romanian production sectors, with disastrous consequences for the fragile balance of the labour market, but also for the budget of romania. it's time for romanian producers to... madam president, today the european commission published a study on the recruitment and retention policies of medical staff in europe. the current migration of health workers from central, eastern and, more recently, southern european countries to countries such as france, italy, germany or the nordic countries, due firstly to financial reasons, then to better working conditions and access to state-of-the-art medical equipment and technologies, raises the awareness of health systems in these countries of origin and, by default, represents a risk factor for patient safety. health labour migration creates a shortage of health personnel and, together with unequal access to innovative treatments, financial barriers that block the effective application of the right to cross-border health, outlines the european union of health inequalities. i believe it is time to put migration and the shortage of medical staff on the european agenda. we need policies for retaining medical staff within the union and a balance of migration within the member states.

member of the commission.– madam president, i wish to thank mr melo for his report. it certainly offers me an opportunity to briefly address some of the issues that have been raised in relation to fruit and vegetables here. the russian import ban has been mentioned by a number of speakers in respect of european fruit and vegetables. it once again highlights the vulnerability of the sector, where surpluses of perishable products can cause large market disturbances and falling producer prices. i am examining this issue at the moment to see what can be done to assist producers. it also shows the importance of strong producer organisations to collectively deal with such unexpected and adverse situations. the current cmo regulation offers the tools for strengthening their bargaining position vis-à-vis major retailers, as well as through production planning, innovation, and crisis prevention and management measures. therefore i welcome mr melo’s report as a contribution to the debate on how producer organisations can be strengthened even further to become even more efficient and also more attractive to both current and future members. the eu fruit and vegetable regime is certainly on the commission’s political agenda. president juncker has asked me to focus on reviewing this potential for further simplification within the first 12 months of our mandate. this meets one of the main requests of this report, which is to increase the attractiveness of producer organisations by increasing legal certainty and reducing the administrative burden. throughout this year the commission will carry out a simplification exercise regarding the fruit and vegetable rules that are contained in the commission-level legislation. this will improve the functioning of the scheme and provide a clearer legal framework. however, we foresee no changes to the basic act this year. producer organisations and their operational programmes thus remain a cornerstone of the regime. the issue of an increase in the overall level of support to producer organisations and to apos, which requires a change in the basic act, will not be addressed as part of this simplification exercise, where we are concentrating on secondary legislation. unfair trading practices in the food supply chain are also on our agenda, as you know. for abuses of relative bargaining power, or unfair trading practices as they are known, there is currently no regulatory framework at eu level, but a large number of member states have now begun to regulate the issue at national level, particularly in the united kingdom and spain. i will continue to work with ms bieńkowska, who is the commissioner for the internal market, industry, entrepreneurship and smes and the lead commissioner on this issue, in order to address issues that have been brought to the attention of this house tonight, and on other occasions, relating to unfair trading practices. the commission has asked the food chain to agree on a self-regulatory mechanism at eu level for the moment. all food chain representatives agreed on a list of principles of good practice in contractual relations as far back as 2011. furthermore, key stakeholders have been implementing an eu-wide voluntary scheme, the supply chain initiative, since the end of 2013, but regrettably not all actors in the food chain are participating at the moment. the commission will make an assessment of existing national and eu work streams and unfair practices at the end of this year and come to conclusions about where to go from there. let me welcome again the european parliament’s initiative and mr melo’s report, which will of course further enrich the ongoing debate regarding the reform that is required in the fruit and vegetables regime.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the proposal to amend the regulation of the european parliament and of the council adopting union procedures in the field of the common commercial policy with a view to ensuring the exercise by the union of the rights conferred on it by the rules of international trade, in particular those established under the auspices of the world trade organisation (wto), as it is intended to codify this regulation exclusively. the world trade organisation (wto) is an international organisation that oversees a large number of agreements defining the 'rules of trade' between member states. the wto is the successor to the general agreement on tariffs and trade and works towards reducing and eliminating barriers to international trade. given that the consultative working party of the legal services of the european parliament, the council and the commission considers that the proposal in question is limited to a simple codification of existing texts without substantive changes to them, i consider that this report should be supported, in order to make the process of unification and standardisation work better.

in writing. ‒ the institutional set-up of the european communities has, since their foundation, been a form of support for free trade between member states. on the basis of this principle, the european union has made a key contribution to the creation of the world trade organisation, the forum for regulating trade relations based on free trade worldwide. however, there are also a number of obstacles in this area, raised by certain third countries, which affect the commercial interests of the european union. in order to overcome these obstacles, the european council adopted regulation (ec) no 3286/94 to give european producers and member states the right to challenge unfair practices in free trade. the regulation respects the practices for the settlement of trade disputes established under the wto. however, this document has become insufficient in the current context of the eu's institutional development. this resolution, which codifies the council regulation in an updated form, thus giving it new legitimacy before the union's trading partners and, more generally, before the wto members, should therefore be adopted.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the proposal as it contains a straightforward codification of the existing texts without any change in their substance.

in writing. ‒ the european union is one of the world's leading shipbuilding producers. in the current competitive world market in this field, there is a need for the european institutions to protect the pursuit of this activity within the union. unfortunately, the existing rules of the world trade organisation, inherited from the defunct gatt, do not ensure that manufacturers are adequately compensated for the damage caused by dumping from a number of countries or even member states. council regulation (ec) no 385/96 fills this legislative gap at global and european level by regulating the pricing practices of ships, at least at european union level. in the event of injury to european shipbuilding producers, it shall be covered by the imposition of duties, countermeasures and equivalent measures on manufacturers who do not comply with the relevant rules. this is a well-deserved protection for the shipbuilding industry against unfair competition practices. however, the council regulation needs to be codified in line with the new legislative requirements of the european institutions, in particular the european parliament. i believe that the adoption of this report will strengthen european regulations in this area and safeguard the european union's much-needed shipbuilding industry.

in writing. ‒ draft amending budget no 4 of 2015 (dab 4/2015) relates to the mobilisation of the eu’s solidarity fund (eusf) for romania, bulgaria and italy for a total amount of eur 66.5 million in commitment and payment appropriations. the eusf provides relief to countries affected by natural disasters and shows solidarity with the population in regions hit by disasters. given the surplus in the eu budget, as presented in draft amending budget no 3/2015, seven eusf cases could have easily been paid for from the 2014 budget. that is particularly important, as the eusf aims to enable a rapid, efficient and flexible response to emergency situations. however, during the budgetary negotiations for 2015, the council insisted on shifting the payments related to the mobilisation of the eusf in draft amending budgets no 5/2014 and no 7/2014 to the 2015 budget for a total amount of eur 126.7 million. while this approach has created a delay in the transfer of the funds, i welcome the link established between dab 3/2015 and dab 4/2015, since it will ensure the common adoption of these two dossiers and the mobilisation of the necessary resources to these countries. for this reason i voted in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ the commission proposed to apply a percentage of 2,5% of the total direct damage in all four cases, as none of them exceeded the respective thresholds for major natural disasters. this is in line with previous practice for regional natural disasters and disasters accepted under the 'neighbouring eligible state' principle. the first mobilisation decision in 2015 was to amend the 2015 budget by increasing the budget under article 13 06 01 (european union solidarity fund member states) by eur 66 505 850 in both commitment and payment appropriations to be entered in the budget outside the mff ceilings. i voted in favour of the proposal for a decision of the european parliament and of the council on the mobilisation of the european union solidarity fund, as these floods have caused direct damage to public and private infrastructure, housing and agriculture and financial assistance from the eusf is vital in view of the major natural disasters that have occurred throughout 2014.
in writing. ‒ i welcome the mobilisation of the european union solidarity fund in the context of the floods in romania (spring and summer 2014), bulgaria (summer 2014) and italy (autumn 2014) under point 11 of the interinstitutional agreement of 2 december 2013.

in writing. ‒ the current report concerns the mobilisation of the eu solidarity fund (eusf) for a total amount of eur 66.5 million eur in commitment and payment appropriations in response to four cases of flooding in romania (two cases), bulgaria and italy in the course of 2014. in all four cases there has been considerable damage to public and private infrastructure, businesses, private homes and assets, the agricultural sector and the environment. the damage led the commission to propose applying the rate of 2.5% of total direct damage in all four cases. given the fact that the eusf aims to provide a rapid, efficient and flexible response to emergency situations, i welcome the recommendation in the report to approve the commission proposal for a decision on the mobilisation of the fund to these countries. taking into account that almost one year has passed since these regions were hit by the floods, it is vital to transfer these funds without further delay. i voted in favour of this report and i hope its adoption will provide the necessary relief to the citizens living in these areas who were affected by the floods.

in writing. ‒ european transport policy is facing many challenges. in addition to questions related to sustainability, economic viability, energy efficiency and environmental sustainability, questions arise about how to respond to traffic congestion, traffic jams and other traffic problems. providing multimodal information, travel planning and ticketing services throughout the eu is an important part of the answer to all these questions. i voted in favour of the european parliament's motion for a resolution on integrated multimodal ticketing in europe because the provision of multimodal information, travel planning and ticketing services at eu level offers opportunities for innovation to european businesses, in particular smes and start-ups, and therefore represents a major contribution to the achievement of a globally competitive european single market and the completion of the single european transport area.
in writing. ‒ support efforts to establish a fair and comprehensive system of travel information and planning so that travellers can access that information on the websites of the services concerned. however, i believe that certain regions or countries are not adequately covered on the existing portals in terms of the options for the different modes and possibilities of transport, which makes cross-border travel more difficult. the information available should enable eu citizens to choose the most sustainable, cheap and fast connection without harming the commercial interests of operators and supports the rapporteur's position that it is the commission's task to identify the appropriate means to this end and to ensure that such access to information does not lead to a dominant position of a provider and therefore to the emergence of a monopoly which would significantly undermine the competitiveness of other market players.
in writing. ‒ there is still a long way to go before a europe-wide, interoperable, compatible and continuous real-time traffic information service is a reality but the evolution of the internet and smartphones make such a service both possible and very necessary. therefore i welcome the commission’s establishment, by way of a delegated act, of specifications for ensuring eu-wide accessibility and the exchange and further development of real-time traffic information services. this is a sound step in the right direction but further steps must be taken so as to enable people making a journey in europe to identify the most sustainable, fastest or best-value multimodal door-to-door travel option, to book and pay for it and then to be informed, both before setting off and during their journey, about any disruption to it and, where applicable, to receive suggestions for alternative routes.

in writing. ‒ i believe that the report on the issue of multimodal integrated tickets in europe, through its modernising contribution, will stimulate the mobility of european citizens. the introduction of an integrated system of travel planning and ticketing services is a response to the challenges facing the european transport sector, ensuring sustainability and improving the safety and security of means of transport. the creation of an integrated ticket, which can be used regardless of the number of modes of transport used during a journey, can make european destinations more accessible and can significantly contribute to the development of continental tourism. i believe that the provision of multimodal information, travel planning and ticketing services throughout the eu facilitates mobility across the european union, a basic condition for the exercise of fundamental freedoms, and contributes to a greater use of public transport, with the car being the means of transport chosen by 72,2% of travellers in 2012. these services can lead to the creation of a single european transport area. i therefore voted in favour of the report.

in writing. ‒ over the last 20 years, the common agricultural policy (cap) has reduced the regulation of agricultural markets, allowing market forces to steer production. this general approach was applied specifically to the fruit and vegetables scheme, where instruments such as export refunds or the setting of minimum prices that processors were obliged to pay to farmers for certain products were abandoned. the union has combined this process of liberalisation with a policy of strengthening producer organisations (po), to give farmers the opportunity to act to protect their interests, for example by selling their products collectively or increasing their added value by processing them on the farm. the 2007 reform of the fruit and vegetables regime confirmed and extended the policy of strengthening the role of producer organisations and associations of producer organisations (apos).
in writing. ‒ i believe that both the european commission and the member states need to develop existing actions or establish new actions, including training measures and the exchange of good practices, which can improve the management of producer organisations and their competitive position in the food supply chain, and i stress the need to review the legislation in force in order to ensure better targeting of producer organisations in all member states.

in writing. ‒ fruits and vegetables are a staple food for the health of european citizens. at the european union level, however, there is modest support for this sector, whose development has been left to the free market. since 2007, however, there has been an increase in support for the fruit and vegetables sector through european agricultural programmes. the economic crisis has halted this positive development, neutralizing the beneficial effects of the policies implemented in recent years. there has even been a deficit in fruit production compared to vegetables within member states, although there are important differences from case to case. this was coupled with the russian embargo on eu fruit and vegetable exports, which deepened the existing crisis. the resolution proposes a number of remedies to these problems, including support for producer associations, investment in human resources in the field, environmental protection measures, measures to support producers in crisis or against abusive practices by supermarket chains. for these reasons, this document should be supported, because it supports a sector that is so important to our citizens.

mr president, i should like to begin by thanking the rapporteur, mr fernandes, for having taken account of the opinion expressed by the committee on foreign affairs on the european commission's budget proposal. i would also like to express my satisfaction at the significant increase in both payment appropriations and commitment appropriations for the european union's external policy in the commission's draft budget. if the union is to have a say on the international scene, it must give itself the means to achieve its ambitions. it is therefore essential that the additional budgetary resources provided for in the budget proposed by the commission be preserved in the final budget. these increases are particularly important for payment appropriations, otherwise a whole series of union programmes, such as the instrument contributing to stability and peace, will find it difficult to resume their activities, which have been partially suspended for financial reasons. in foreign policy, our parliament will continue to be committed to the neighbourhood both to the south and to the east, and it seems to me therefore essential that a european neighbourhood instrument should be endowed with sufficient means so that we can support the countries around us. i also think it is important that this year's budget reflects our commitment to respect for human rights and democracy in our neighbourhood and beyond. i hope therefore that the final budget will reflect these two concerns which are at the heart of our foreign policy.
mr president, the european parliament comes to this trilogue with a clear and firm vision of how we think about the european budget. it is very important to us that the budgetary strategy of the european union is focused on development and investment that will ensure a better life for european citizens. in this context, our message is simple: we must have a budget that goes beyond the logic of austerity and focuses on investing in people, in european projects and programmes dedicated to job creation, in those aimed at vocational training, in those supporting the development of smes, in those supporting the development of european democracy and our active role in promoting our values. we therefore expect the european commission to be more clear, efficient and transparent in spending european public money, and we expect, in particular, the european council, which we see still lacking today, to be able to sustain commitments for a european budget that meets the expectations of the citizens it is supposed to represent.
mr president, commissioner, you will negotiate the 2016 budget with mr fernandez - you know him very well, you negotiated the efsi with him and in the end, a very good regulation came out. the 2016 budget - i think it's a budget to say 'of reference' because it will be the first payments from the structural funds. you have to make the payments to cover the debts to cohesion policy - there are a lot of them, over 25 billion - and at the same time i think there has to be the recovery of the money for horizon 2020 and the esf. so you have a complicated negotiation. you've seen the warrant, it's a solid warrant. fernandez has built it very well, and the expectations at the end of these negotiations are very high. i hope these negotiations don't, as usual, be until the last night, when the council says "that's it" and everyone has to agree, because otherwise we don't have the budget. i think that if we do not reach a balance in the budget, meeting the three conditions to pay debts, to take account of payments for cohesion policy 2014-2020 and at the same time to ensure the recovery of funds taken by the efsi from the two important programmes we have to experience one thing: not having a budget for 2016.

madam president, the threats to the internal security of the european union are increasing every day. many have become unconventional, asymmetrical, fast-moving and unpredictable. each member state must defend its internal and external security, but the union must also have its own security strategy to be implemented together with the member states. and trust is very important here - trust between the member states and trust of the union in each member state. there is still no real european governance of the common area of freedom, security and justice that is the european union. there is no common defence policy and no european army to intervene to keep the peace when it is threatened in a member state or in a neighbouring country. the european agenda on security, which we are discussing today, and i congratulate the commission on its adoption, has three priorities. the first priority is to fight terrorism and to stop european citizens from joining terrorist groups. another priority is the fight against cybercrime and a third priority is the fight against cross-border organised crime. organized crime finances terrorism, arms terrorist groups and infiltrates the economy. the european anti-fraud office and the joint investigation teams shall work as quickly as possible on the territory of the union. it is vital to confiscate the money used, derived from organised crime. black money that flows freely creates death and brings terrorism. we save lives by fighting organized crime and confiscating money.

member of the commission, on behalf of the vice-president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy.– mr president, it is a pleasure to present to this house today, on behalf of vice-president/high representative mogherini, our annual report on human rights and democracy in the world 2014. the annual report tells the story of the work the eu has done on human rights and democracy during the past year, both bilaterally with our partners worldwide and multilaterally. the year 2014 has been a year of unprecedented challenges to human rights. the world has not seen so many people fleeing conflict since the second world war. almost 60 million people are displaced worldwide. these millions of people fleeing their homes to find refuge from violence and economic hardship are an easy prey to violations of human rights. finding an appropriate response to the manifold issues arising from these dire circumstances is often not easy. to ensure that the human rights of migrants are duly respected, we need to address all parts of the chain, providing immediate measures to save lives and fight traffickers while at the same time working on long-term strategies to tackle the root causes. the threat of terrorism poses an ever-growing challenge to our free and open societies, but we need to ensure that counter-terrorism activities are guided by the same principles that formed the foundation of our democratic societies. respect for human rights is central in this regard. in the end, our ability to achieve sustainable improvements on human rights worldwide will also depend on our own ability to live by, and adhere to, these standards. cooperation with this parliament is one of the guardians of democratic principles and values and is therefore of utmost importance to us. in our concerted efforts to find solutions to the most pressing human rights concerns, the eu has taken action in multiple ways, and our report bears witness to that. it underscores the extensive work done by the network of eu delegations worldwide in following cases of human rights violations, meeting the lawyers of jailed human rights defenders, attending trials as observers and leading local, political and human rights dialogues with the authorities. in short, by being on the front line in defending people whose human rights are violated. in 2014 we held human rights dialogues and consultations with nearly 40 partner countries. in addition, many of the 79 african, caribbean and pacific countries that are part of the cotonou agreement conducted a dialogue with the eu, during which human rights issues in cases were raised. at the same time, the implementation of the 132 human rights country strategies has resulted in more intense collaboration between the eu delegations and member states embassies on the ground and has led to more coherent human rights dialogues. our main financial instrument in the area of human rights – the european instrument for democracy and human rights – has continued to support civil society organisations and human rights defenders worldwide. we have also strengthened our capacity to act in a coherent and effective manner by adopting guidelines on freedom of opinion and expression online and offline, and on freedom of religion and belief. the eu has reiterated its strong commitment to preventing and eradicating torture worldwide and has systematically raised individual cases during human rights dialogues, besides calling for the introduction of specific national prevention mechanisms. during the last year, we remained strongly committed to protecting children from violence, exploitation, abuse and neglect. the eu pledged more than eur 100 million for the next seven years to gender equality and children’s wellbeing, including concrete projects on ending female genital mutilation and child, early and forced marriage. the crucial role of our special representative for human rights – and i am happy that stavros lamprinidis is with us today – in increasing the overall coherence, effectiveness and visibility of human rights in eu foreign policy cannot be highlighted enough. the year 2014 also marked the end of our first long-term policy on human rights, the action plan on human rights and democracy for 2012 to 2014, which has allowed the overall coherence and coordination of eu activities in the field of human rights to be improved. progress could also be achieved in mainstreaming human rights across all eu policies and promoting greater coherence in our action towards third countries. not least thanks to your valuable proposals, we managed to make remarkable progress in defining a new, ambitious, long-term policy document for promoting and protecting human rights worldwide in the next five years. i am happy to announce to the house today that, together with member states, we are finalising the new action plan on human rights and democracy for the years 2015-2019. it will aim at substantive further progress in implementing the eu strategy adopted in 2012. it includes multiple dedicated actions focusing on those areas that require renewed political commitment and additional efforts. we intend in particular to concentrate on, firstly, empowering local actors and encouraging indigenous forces in a spirit of partnership, and secondly on addressing human rights challenges in key areas. these include freedom of expression, freedom of religion, anti-discrimination, gender equality, children’s rights, combating torture and promoting economic, social and cultural rights. certainly we want to tackle and redress human rights violations in conflicts and crises. further, we want to foster the coherence of the eu response in strategic policy areas such as migration, trade and counterterrorism. finally, we want to deepen our effectiveness and improve the results of our tools. i am aware that this is a rather ambitious agenda. it will be the agenda for human rights in the coming years. looking back on our activities, we have already come a long way. despite the severe challenges that still remain, we should not underestimate the progress already achieved, hence our increased and concerted commitment for sustainable long-term solutions to the current complex and diverse challenges. we will continue to speak out on injustice and human rights violations all around the world. we will continue to challenge others as much as we challenge ourselves, and we will continue to critically assess our own approach and actions and, where necessary, adjust them. your scrutiny is central and indispensable in this regard.

implementation of the eu's strategic framework and action plan on the same issue. this is of course a very positive development, because we need to take the time to reflect on what we are doing, day by day, to promote human rights and democracy. the 2014 annual report makes me wonder if the interpretation of the term 'implementation' is too narrow. this year's report, which is almost 400 pages conferences on human rights, etc. i believe that the report should go further in the understanding of the term 'implementation' and that it should also address the difficulties and, of course, the content of the annual report, that i think it would be important to emphasize our policy of support for democracy more, because it seems to me to be secondary to human rights. in reality, democracy and human rights are closely linked. the most basic rights of any individual are far more likely to be respected in a democratic system than in any other.

resolution strategy. i also agree with your conclusion: to effectively deal with this challenge, the european union and its member states must think strategically in the medium and long term. we must radicalisation. mostly this is about providing opportunities to the youngest members of society. young people must be inspired by values that reject violence, create peace and build inclusive, open play in society. all communities must be given a chance to contribute to the social, economic and political life of their own countries. entire religious and ethnic groups – christians and others – religion but a struggle for power and regional hegemony. the eu is doing all it can to halt and prevent this violence. we will not let sectarianism prevail. moreover, i fully agree that the engagement and empowerment of women in the public, political, economic and cultural spheres is key to fostering stability, peace and economic prosperity in the long run. women’s rights and gender equality must be basic components of the political and human rights dialogue between the eu and the mena countries. the eu is committed to ensuring that human rights are mainstreamed in all its activities. since 2012, the eu has engaged regularly with the league of arab states, including the arab human rights charter committee and the arab national human rights institutions. as you rightly point out, in the past the european neighbourhood policy sometimes failed to adequately take into account the specificities of each of our partners, including with regard to identifying civil society partners needing support and capacity-building assistance. the review of the neighbourhood policy that is on the way is an opportunity to introduce changes that will help the eu to be a stronger player. we intend to in writing.– for decades, the middle east has been dominated by the arab-israeli conflict. the muslim communities in the major eu countries have naturally been affected by these ups and downs, in turn, influencing the diplomatic position of those countries – consequently, of the eu – on the conflict itself and the attempts to find a durable solution to it. coupled with the radicalization generated by the current world economic and financial crisis, the number of anti-semitic manifestations in western europe has increased and the official eu positions on the arab-israeli conflict got tougher in consequence. the reality is much more complex: the middle east and north africa have become the object of a border-breaking process: libya, syria, iraq and yemen have now, for all practical reasons, fluctuating borders, nobody knowing how they will look in the future. the attempts of isil – a product of an intra-muslim bitter conflict – of filling the vacuum thus created is already contributing to the radicalisation of the eu muslim communities, displacing the old arab-israeli conflict as the number one cause of it. consequently, the eu should revise its traditional perception centred around the latter, refocusing instead on the redrawing of borders in the arab world.
member of the commission.– mr president, thank you once again for giving me a break; this is old collegiality between commissioners. i would also like to thank all of you for the opportunity to come and discuss with you the review of the european neighbourhood policy (enp) and i am particularly grateful to eduard kukan and also to the shadow rapporteurs for their hard work in bringing together the views of the committee on foreign affairs on such an important issue. we have just come to the end of our public consultation on the enp review based on the joint communication we published in march. the vice-president/high representative, myself and our teams have held consultations with member states, national parliaments, partner countries, civil society, social partners, local and regional government, businesses, think tanks and academia. it is not often that europe’s foreign policy is opened up to such a widespread debate. of course, consultation, views and advice from parliament have been a key part of this process, and i have greatly appreciated the opportunity for me and also my officials to meet you on several occasions to share information and ideas. in the consultation there has been a great consensus that events in the eastern neighbourhood and in the southern mediterranean demand a new approach to the enp. we need to rethink our approach and put our partnership on a new footing. your own reflections have underlined the need for greater differentiation in the way we work with partners. this is a principle that has found a positive echo among our partners and with member states. we need to find the right formula for each of our partners in a way that serves our own interests and theirs. it is clearer now even than it was at the start of the review that we need to work closely with our neighbours on common challenges such as migration, terrorism, extremism and energy security. this year, 2015, has given us ample proof that this partnership cannot be a one-way street but must be one based on mutual interests and need. some of these partners are seeking a close integration with us and some do not currently have this aspiration. this is the reality to which we must adapt our policy. we need to identify how we can show our relevance to this diverse range of partners while at the same time remaining true to our fundamentals. our aim is a prosperous stable neighbourhood. we will continue to support democracy, the rule of law, human rights, and efficient and accountable public institutions as essential ingredients for the neighbourhood we want to see. when i visit our partner countries i make a point of ensuring that i visit civil society organisations. i believe that they play an essential role both in ensuring accountability and the fair development of their societies and in providing vital advice to the european union. where we have successful cooperation in place we should pursue it, but we will aim to be more responsive and more flexible in how we can support those wrestling with painful reforms. we will work harder to make sure that our support is coordinated so that each country can draw maximum benefit from the help on offer from the eu and its member states. where partner countries want a more focused agenda of cooperation, we should be ready to offer this. i believe there are some key areas that are emerging as the natural focus for some of our partners: economic growth and decent job opportunities, particularly for the young; promoting business links in targeted sectors; circular migration that offers opportunity without draining talent permanently away from home, alongside the continuing efforts to tackle the challenges of irregular migration. we must do all we can to make sure that all our foreign policy and security tools are brought together to help resolve conflict and develop the resilience of our partners. where we can, we must reach out for partners beyond the neighbourhood who share the eu’s interest in stability and development. so i am looking forward to hearing your views on these and other key elements of the review.

mr. chairman, long-term shareholder engagement and corporate governance will drive long-term investment. the financial crisis highlighted shareholders' excessive short-term risk-taking, which led to the bankruptcy of many companies. the proposal voted on makes european companies much more attractive by offering incentives to shareholders through special voting rights and dividends. the managers will also be required to disclose all information concerning potential conflicts of interest, investment strategy, turnover. citizens need to know why a company has raised or lowered a price. the voting of the director's salary policy by the general meeting of shareholders is also introduced as a mandatory requirement. that's how we make sure a ceo doesn't pay his own salary. transparency is the key against tax fraud and conflict of interest.
in writing. ‒ encouraging shareholder participation in corporate governance of companies is intended to increase their financial performance, hold decisions accountable and, at the same time, advance the particular interests of companies. to that end, a balance needs to be struck between the exercise of shareholder rights, confidentiality and the protection of personal data. furthermore, the commission should present clear rules on the establishment of specific requirements for the transmission of information on the identity of shareholders. i voted in favour of this report because i believe that more active participation of shareholders in companies helps to increase the transparency of the decision-making process and to strengthen the dialogue.
in writing. ‒ based on our s&d values, i believe that the report on shareholders’ rights directive approved in the legal affairs committee with the support of our group, will improve economic stability, foster long-term shareholding and boost long-term investment. i support the idea that it is a necessary instrument in order to ensure more transparency in company management and in the activity of financial intermediaries. in particular, it sets the mechanism and the policy on directors’ remuneration with yearly reporting on its implementation. i would also like to welcome the importance of the report in fighting tax evasion and tax avoidance, and most importantly, the introduction of the country-by-country reporting obligation on taxes paid for large and listed companies. i would like to thank and praise the rapporteur sergio gaetano cofferati as well as the shadow rapporteurs for the great job done.
in writing. ‒ this is a very important file. the objectives of the revision of the shareholders’ rights directive are to improve stability and to boost long-term investment. the report introduces country-by-country reporting on taxes paid for large and listed companies. multinationals would have to break their information down by country of operation so that citizens and operations can see where large companies actually pay their taxes. it is our duty to fight against tax havens and for tax justice.
in writing. ‒ i have voted for this report that will sustain greater involvement of shareholders in companies’ corporate governance.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report and i deeply support the initiative to better encourage long-term shareholder engagement in their respective investments. their rights and influence in businesses and companies need to be properly safeguarded and new ways need to exist to ensure a better engagement of shareholders, at more market levels, in the major decisions of the companies they are invested in. this can only improve competition and development and should be seen as a positive step towards better financial and non-financial performance of companies!
in writing. tax transparency is one of the objectives taken on by the european parliament, including through this resolution. we need to get to a deeper level of integration when it comes to corporate taxation in europe. the right principle of international companies paying taxes where they make their profits can change the tax paradigm in europe. reporting at the level of each member state of profit made, subsidies received and taxes paid is essential to increase the quality of public information available to shareholders of large enterprises, public authorities and, not least, european citizens in the areas where corporations operate. corporate social responsibility must not remain an expression. it must become a way of operating for cross-border businesses that operate and make a profit in europe. i voted for this resolution because i am a supporter of fair taxation in europe and the elimination of tax fraud and evasion. i am convinced that transparency is a necessary but not sufficient step towards effective and fair taxation for all eu member states.

in writing. ‒ i voted against the report on the eu scheme for greenhouse gas emission allowance trading, as it is against the interests of romania and romanian citizens. romania supported this mechanism in the form proposed by the commission, whereby the price was set automatically and transparently, and it was to enter into force in 2021. however, the amendments introduced in the negotiations between the european parliament and the council are contrary to the national interest and will affect all sectors of industry in romania by increasing the price of these certificates. the free allocation of these certificates to the top 10% of installations at eu level means that romanian industries, without strong financial resources and without state-of-the-art technologies, will have to buy them from the market at a very high price. in this respect, i supported romania's position in these negotiations and voted against this report.

in writing. ‒ the eu carbon market must be a fair system which does not disproportionately affect some member states. those countries with large tertiary sectors are less exposed to the effects of the ets, whilst countries like romania with an important manufacturing base face higher costs and usually have fewer resources to protect against carbon leakage. the existing compensation measures, including article 10c of the ets directive and the so-called ‘solidarity allowances’, are not enough if the carbon price is to be increased by withholding credits from the market. however, if harmonised compensation for indirect costs were to be introduced at eu level, a fairer system could be developed.

in writing. ‒ up to 20 million jobs could be created by 2020 thanks to the 'green economy' initiative. the definition of the concept of 'green jobs' has created a current of contradictions at european level, especially in the attempt to use this concept for statistical purposes. a 'green' job is a decent job that has the potential to reduce energy and raw material consumption, limit greenhouse gas emissions, minimise waste and pollution, and protect and restore ecosystems. i voted for this report because we need a comprehensive response to ensure that we can maintain and expand employment opportunities and green job creation. time is a key factor, as we are missing opportunities and failing to provide our workforce with all the skills needed to tackle the challenges we already face. the commission's communication provides some answers, but it will take all the eu institutions to play their part in order to really achieve this necessary transition to a greener economy.

in writing. ‒ i believe it is very important to outline the employment challenges and opportunities of the current transition towards a green, low-carbon, energy and resource-efficient economy. the green employment initiative communication presents an integrated framework to allow labour market and skill policies to play an active role to support this transition and focuses on the importance of anticipating and establishing adequate skills policies to support workers in coping with structural change, of securing labour market transitions, and of strengthening governance and partnership-based initiatives. this is a positive report which supports the commission approach regarding the transition towards a greener economy.
