in writing. ‒ the european union is one of the world's largest energy-consuming actors. for this reason, member states are constantly looking for new energy sources with the highest possible efficiency. this objective can be better achieved within a european energy union, which provides a framework for the coordination of member states' energy policies. the european commission's strategy for the energy union is based on the five dimensions of energy security, the integrated common energy market, energy efficiency, decarbonisation of the economy and research and innovation. while diversification of sources is imperative for energy security, in terms of energy efficiency and decarbonisation of the economy, more ambitious renewable energy targets and the gradual reduction of the use of polluting fuels should be considered. particular attention should be paid to research and innovation in this area, because we need the best solutions to support our citizens. the completion of an integrated european energy common market will create the framework for competitive and favourable prices for both small and large consumers, to the benefit of us all.
in writing. ‒ the european union is currently the world's leading energy importer, importing 53% of the energy it consumes, at an annual cost of around €400 billion. old energy infrastructures, weak integration of energy markets, lack of coordination of national energy policies generally lead to consumers and businesses not having a wide range of options or lower prices. the commission also found that the chinese exporting producers were not able to obtain sufficient spare capacity to meet the demand for electricity from the union industry. in addition to uncompetitive energy prices and extremely high dependence on third country suppliers, climate change is threatening the sustainability of the european energy system. improving energy interconnections between member states and modernising infrastructure would help to limit energy dependency and the risk of supply disruptions. moreover, the construction of a common energy market would facilitate access to energy markets across national borders. this would ensure secure and sustainable energy sources and affordable prices for eu citizens and businesses. i therefore voted in favour of the report entitled 'towards a european energy union'.
in writing. ‒ the report on the preparation of europe's electricity network for 2020 underlines the importance of a forward-looking policy, in which the union commits to increasing electricity interconnection to 10% by 2020. this is a valuable objective, setting a safe and sustainable direction for the electricity system. at present, 12 member states, mainly located at the periphery of the union, remain below the 10% interconnection target and are isolated from the internal electricity market. i voted in favour of this report because a concerted effort is needed to support member states whose low level of connectivity prevents the completion of the internal market in electricity from meeting this objective. as a result, a diligent determination to achieve the set objectives and intensified work in the groups advised on this issue is needed.
in writing. ‒ the 10% electricity interconnection target, first set in 2002 on the basis of the electricity generation capacity then existing, is to be achieved by 2020. the 10% target does not reflect the quantity of electricity transferred between countries, nor its quality, such as the availability of existing interconnection infrastructure or existing national infrastructure between interconnections. there are still 12 member states, mainly located in the eu's peripheral regions, which still remain below the 10% threshold and are therefore heavily isolated from the internal electricity market. i support the ep's motion for a resolution because i believe that renewable energy, energy efficiency and a sustainable energy mix that leads to energy savings and leads to an internal energy market that allows the free flow of energy are important means for a stable, independent, secure, transparent, inclusive and competitive energy system in the eu, which generates quality jobs in a sustainable, future-oriented economy. consider the creation of such a system and the elimination of energy islands as a major political priority of the european union.

in writing. ‒ this report is in response to a commission communication describing measures needed to meet the agreed target to ensure all member states have in place sufficient electricity interconnectors with neighbouring countries with capacity to export/import at least 10% of their electricity generation capacity. it was a target originally set by eu heads of state and government in 2002 and should be reached by 2020. some eight member states are still to meet the target. we need strong political support and new measures to ensure europe’s electricity network is properly connected in order to avoid member states being isolated, ensure a true internal energy market as part of the energy union and bring down the costs of integrating renewable energy into the grid.

in writing. ‒ an interconnected european electricity system would bring electricity prices down, reduce productivity losses in the commercial and industrial sectors and stimulate the growth of the european renewable energy industry. for these reasons, the european council established that member states should reach an electricity interconnection target of at least 10% of their installed capacity with their eu neighbours. in light of this goal, the european parliament drafted a report that highlights a list of issues that are crucial for the achievement of this target. these refer to the need for a faster permitting process for high voltage lines, better targeted investment and improved member state cooperation at regional level. i do believe this report has the right focus and therefore my vote was in favour.

in writing. ‒ the 2013 reform of the common fisheries policy (cfp) included among its objectives the achievement of maximum sustainable yield, applying an ecosystem approach. the main instruments for achieving these objectives are technical measures and multiannual plans. however, despite the benefits of these two instruments, little progress has been made since 2009. the multiannual plans encountered an interinstitutional deadlock and the technical measures were lacking in legislation. the new common fisheries policy brings an improvement to these two instruments. the technical measures are thus based on three geographically distinct sets of measures which are transposed into specific sets of rules, and the multiannual plans aim at managing the main species of interest for fishing, integrating concrete measures to implement them. given the importance of these instruments in the common fisheries policy, i voted in favour of this report.
in writing. ‒ i believe that the new cfp framework regulation on technical measures needs to be formulated in a clear manner, which will require a significant effort of clarification.
in writing. ‒ technical measures and multiannual plans are essential instruments to achieve the objectives of the 2013 cfp reform. the revised technical measures regulation must ensure clarity and legal certainty. it should seek to improve the conservation and sustainable exploitation of stocks and implement the ecosystem-based approach to fisheries management in a way that is consistent with the socio-economic viability of the fisheries sector. it is important to highlight the positive aspects of ending the wasteful practice of discarding as well as available emff support. i believe we must support strongly the call for a solid scientific approach to improving the conservation and sustainable exploitation of stocks, minimising the impact on the marine environment, fighting iuu fishing, supporting fishermen, in particular traditional sustainable fishing practices and small-scale fishing, training, innovation, research, involvement of all relevant stakeholders in the decision-making, and regular re-evaluation.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report that will ensure the implementation of the common fisheries policy objectives.
in writing. ‒ i have voted for this report regarding the implementation of a new common fisheries policy including necessary technical measures and multi annual plans.
in writing. ‒ i voted for the mato report on the new cfp: the structure of technical measures and multiannual plans. although a new cfp was created in 2013, progress on conservation has been lagging so far. the technical measures are heterogeneous and inconsistent, in particular because they were adopted through different legislative procedures and were in response to very different motivations. in the future, legislators must ensure that technical measures are simple and clear, so that they can be easily understood by fishermen. it is also necessary to find a solution as soon as possible to move forward with the multiannual plans. it is also essential that fishermen are consulted at every step in the revision and implementation of the legislation.
in writing. ‒ the european union gives fisheries a prominent place in its major policies. in 2013, the common fisheries policy was reformed to establish maximum sustainable yield using an ecosystem approach. the main instruments through which the objectives of the new policy can be achieved are technical measures and multiannual plans as conservation measures. however, little progress has been made in implementing these instruments to date, due to the interinstitutional deadlock. in this context, it is necessary to apply without delay the measures required by the reformed system, such as the avoidance of bycatch of juvenile fish and other by-catches, the conservation and sustainable exploitation of existing stocks, the minimisation of the impact on the marine environment, the fight against illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing, the support of traditional fisheries, the support of research and innovation in the field, the involvement of all relevant decision-makers and the periodic reassessment of the policy. the implementation of these measures will have a direct effect on the ability to continue fishing in the future, by allowing the necessary fish stocks to be reproduced and avoiding the depletion of these important marine resources. for these reasons, i consider that the present report should be adopted in order to clarify the rules in this area.

in writing. ‒ mismatches between tax systems create a pathway for tax avoidance by companies, especially multinationals. if we take into account the inefficiency of collection or special tax regimes, together with the profit transfer system, the budgetary losses can reach between eur 160 and 190 billion annually. simply put, we lose 110% of the eu budget every year because of tax evasion. i welcome the approach of the principles of transparency, convergence and transnational coordination. i took part in this vote with the intention of giving the commission the tools it needs to limit as far as possible the losses to national budgets caused by tax avoidance by large companies operating in the eu. i also appreciate the work of the taxe committee, which has succeeded in establishing a number of clear principles, including the introduction of a common corporate tax base. i fully agree that this base should be operational by the end of 2017 at the latest. it is irrational to react to the limitation of public funds for the investment and operation of national and european apparatuses, but at the same time not to make progress in increasing the quality of collection in the budgets that support these investments and institutions.
madam president, it is not an easy task for the eu to sort out the dilemma of how to best deal with china, the second largest economy in the world and its second largest trading partner. but china is also an authoritarian state responsible for serious breaches of fundamental rights, including the freedom of expression, association, assembly and religion. europe needs an approach in which the pursuit of its trade and investment interests does not go against the principles it claims to stand for. it should not ignore issues such as the persecution of buddhist monks and nuns, the ever-increasing number of self-immolations, the forceful resettlement of over 2 million tibetan nomads, the mistreatment of the uighur population, the demolition of christian churches or removal of their crosses, the forced disappearance of hundreds of human rights lawyers and so on. only by dealing with such matters can we build a credible and strong relationship with china; one that is in the interest of both the eu and the population of china.
in writing. ‒ this year marks 40 years since the start of diplomatic relations between the eu and china, which are extremely important for both sides in finding common answers to a range of global issues such as global security, the fight against terrorism, cyber security and climate change. we need to see china as a major trading partner for the union, with a huge, expanding market, but we need to react to the slippages in this country. although the chinese government recognises the importance and universality of human rights, it is unable to demonstrate concrete results in improving the human rights situation. it is unacceptable that in the chinese conception, socioeconomic rights should take precedence over individual civil and political rights. it is also of concern that china is currently the country that executes the most people and continues to carry out the death penalty in secret on thousands of people annually, without regard to minimum international standards on the use of the death penalty. i voted in favour of this report in the belief that the eu's involvement through the council and the commission can have positive results, achieving, through constructive dialogue, the transition of this country towards the rule of law and respect for human rights.
in writing. ‒ i welcome the 40th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the european union and china as a source of inspiration for strengthening the strategic partnership so necessary in a multipolar and globalised world, and i consider china to be an important international power and one of the eu's most important partners. i therefore believe that the two sides must promote the eu-china comprehensive strategic partnership over the next decade that will be beneficial for both the eu and china.
in writing. ‒ china is a major trading partner of the eu, with a huge and expanding market; the ongoing investment agreement negotiations represent one of the most important issues in eu-china bilateral economic and trade relations. i welcome the 40th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the eu and china as a source of inspiration to strengthen the strategic partnership, which is so necessary in a multipolar and globalised world, and to speed up the ongoing negotiations for a new partnership and cooperation agreement based on trust, transparency and respect for human rights. i strongly support the call for finding mutual answers to a range of global concerns and identifying common interests, such as global and regional security, counter-terrorism, the fight against organised crime, cybersecurity, weapons of mass destruction and nuclear non-proliferation, energy security, global financial and market regulation, climate change and sustainable development. i am especially worried about environmental degradation in china, which has taken on dramatic proportions and i believe that more urgent, strong and targeted government action is needed.
in writing. ‒ i have voted in favour of this report that will establish a new connectivity platform with the aim of creating a favourable environment for sustainable and interoperable cross-border infrastructure networks between eu countries and china.
in writing. ‒ i have voted for this report that reiterates the key importance of a strategic partnership between eu and china in order to find mutual answers to global security, financial and market regulation, energy security and climate change, as well as sustainable development of a framework that can respond to bilateral concerns.
in writing. ‒ this report covers the relations between eu and china, which began 40 years ago, covering political, economic, environmental, social and human rights aspects. the report follows a constructive approach that highlights both china’s vigorous economic growth and international importance, and the deficiencies it has yet to overcome. initially, the report calls for enhanced coordination and cooperation between the eu and china in areas of strategic significance, such as security, climate change, sustainable development, market governance and regulation. the report also states the eu’s support for an open human rights dialogue between the eu and china based on mutual respect. the report also takes account of the tensions in the south china sea by asking all parties to avoid provocative actions that lead to escalations, and instead to favour peaceful settlements of disputes according to international laws and arbitration. china is a significant partner for the eu, and i believe the current report represents the importance of open and constructive relationships between the sides. i also believe that the current document can help defining the cooperation line for the eu with china; for this reason i voted in favour of the report.
in writing. ‒ currently, 250 million people are affected by humanitarian crises and over 60 million people are forcibly displaced. these are numbers that cannot leave us indifferent and that call for more and more humanitarian responses around the world. given that by 2050 one billion people are likely to be displaced as a result of climate change, concerted action is needed and there is a need to build trust and to expand cooperation between private sector groups, ngos, local authorities, international organisations and governments. i have spoken in favour of this report because, as the world's leading donor and key humanitarian actor, the eu has a responsibility to take a leading role in exploiting more efficient and effective means to meet the needs of people affected by conflict and disaster.
in writing. ‒ globally, humanitarian responses are increasingly needed as a result of the challenges posed by rapid population growth, demographic change, urbanisation, the increase in the number and severity of natural disasters, environmental degradation, desertification, climate change, long-term and simultaneous conflicts with regional impact, and resource scarcity, coupled with the consequences of poverty, migration, inequalities, forced displacement and vulnerability. the number of people in need has more than doubled since 2004, reaching over 100 million in 2015, and 250 million people are affected by humanitarian crises, while the number of forcibly displaced people has reached almost 60 million, of which 40 million are internally displaced, and over 50% of refugees worldwide are children. i support the ep motion for a resolution on the preparation of the world humanitarian summit (whs). the whs, convened for the first time by the un secretary-general, will take place in istanbul in may 2016. i believe it is imperative to ensure a stronger link between the humanitarian and development sectors and to refocus on prevention and anticipation measures, changing the current humanitarian-based approach.
in writing. ‒ the european union and its member states, as the main donors of humanitarian aid, are key policy-makers with operational experience at global level. the humanitarian system must meet the challenge of providing increased support to as many people as possible at higher costs. in view of the scale of the current crises and disasters, humanitarian aid funds are insufficient, despite the very high level of contributions from donors. in addition to the financial resource, consideration should be given to changing the way the humanitarian community operates in terms of planning, coordination and response capacity. the humanitarian summit must find the best ways to protect civilians, identify threats and monitor violations of human rights and international humanitarian law. the need to provide food, water, shelter, hygiene and medical treatment to those in need is of major importance in humanitarian aid, namely minimum humanitarian standards must be ensured and maintained during the intervention. the right to education should not be ignored, but on the contrary, it should be promoted and supported during protracted humanitarian crises, without which the future of children is threatened.
in writing. ‒ i fully support the rapporteur's position that the european union, as the leading donor and key global humanitarian actor, can generate the necessary leverage and also has a responsibility to take a leading role in exploring more efficient and effective means to meet the needs of people affected by conflict and disaster.
in writing. ‒ i strongly believe that the eu should assume leadership and play a pivotal role in the world humanitarian summit process, towards a strong outcome. the eu should consider the world humanitarian summit as an opportunity to build partnerships and find common ground on humanitarian principles and international standards, and to enhance cooperation and coordination of assistance. more cooperation and complementary is needed between humanitarian and development policies, which should go hand in hand with increased development aid and humanitarian funding. moreover, special protection has to be given to women, children and people with disabilities. specific protection should be provided to children and notably to the facilitation of their access to education during emergencies. i support more involvement and cooperation of the private sector, ngos, local authorities and international organisations in humanitarian actions and the building of partnerships with non-traditional donors.
in writing. ‒ the world is being faced with humanitarian crises, unprecedented both in their number, scale and persistence. i have voted in favour of this report that will continue to emphasise the essential role of the ngos in humanitarian action and to ensure that their views are taken into consideration throughout the process and reflected in the outcome.
in writing. ‒ i have voted for this report that will instate an operational framework for the key stakeholders, the ngos and development communities, with the purpose of creating convergence between humanitarian aid and development policy, in order to reduce and manage future humanitarian risks.
in writing. ‒ the world we live in shows us that humanitarian challenges are constantly emerging. categories forced into a situation of risk or vulnerability by conflict, epidemic, food shortage or natural disaster are increasing. cooperation with the united nations to make humanitarian aid more effective is all the more valuable in this context. a global alliance of innovation for humanitarian purposes is an imperative for the coming period and the eu can be at the forefront of advocating such action. the eu remains the un's main donor and as such, as i have said many times, it must play a leading role in the un's humanitarian and public policies. this includes the formulation of a common and unified position of the member states with regard to the presence at the un. we have to assume that this report is not just about the refugee crisis. the way the eu treats this vulnerable group of displaced people also defines our real attitude towards the humanitarian phenomenon. i support this motion for a resolution and hope that this act will be doubled by firm eu action in the field of humanitarian aid restructuring.
in writing. ‒ approximately 160 000 redundancies occurred in the steel and related sectors. the european base metals industry is currently facing massive investment losses to third countries, which are caused by the comparatively higher level of energy prices and the cost of carbon dioxide emissions. on the other hand, there is a decline in demand in this sector, but also strong global competition from third countries that do not apply the same high standards and strict regulations as those in europe. the paradox is that the capacity reduction in the aluminium sector in europe is taking place against the backdrop of an increase in european demand for aluminium in recent years, which leads to an increase in imports. i support this report because a concrete position and a well-regulated framework are needed because otherwise the closure of factories will lead to the irreversible loss of technologies and technological skills as well as the loss of industrial workforce skills.
in writing. ‒ the steel sector is suffering from the worst peacetime crisis in its history, leading to a high dependence of the industrial production sector on imports from third countries and a loss of industrial technological skills, with a direct impact on millions of jobs (following the reduction of steel production capacities by over 40 million tonnes since 2008 and the loss of over 60 000 direct jobs and over 100 000 indirect jobs). the european base metals industry is facing massive investment losses to third countries, mainly due to the comparatively higher level of energy prices and the cost of carbon dioxide emissions. i support the european parliament's motion for a resolution on the development of a sustainable european base metals industry. i believe that the eu must provide for flexible and reactive trade defence means, adapted to the new global industrial realities, in which decisions are taken in a timely manner, given the possible multiplication of flows of materials and products, as well as information and services.
in writing. ‒ i believe that energy-intensive industries must continue their efforts to optimise recycling mechanisms and reduce co2 emissions, in order to ensure industrial competitiveness in the future and to meet the mandatory reduction targets set by the european union.
in writing. ‒ the haemorrhaging of skills and jobs in the european steel industry is the result of a slump in demand. there have been such significant adjustments in capacity that any upturn in european demand will give rise to an unprecedented trade deficit in europe that would engender dependency and the loss of industrial know-how and is bound to have a knock-on effect on the downstream automotive, construction and low-carbon technologies sectors. on the other hand, closures in the european aluminium industry are taking place at an alarming pace against a backdrop of growing european demand for aluminium in recent years, which has led to increases in imports. steel and aluminium are two prime examples of the difficulties faced by those working in such industries, which must continue to modernise in energy and environmental terms when this means following an investment policy which few can currently afford. thus, while climate change policy is in no way the root cause of the problems facing these industries, it may well be so in the future if the investment crisis continues and if no european industrial policy on raw materials and base metals is implemented.
in writing. ‒ the report highlights the importance of the base metals industry to the eu's internal market and that it influences a number of sectors, including the automotive, aerospace, construction and packaging sectors. all these sectors support hundreds of thousands of jobs and need to be supported. i voted in favour of the report in particular for the calls in the report for the need to support the eu steel industry, through investment and ensuring fair competition in the internal market in relation to non-european steel products entering the internal market. deindustrialization brings with it the disappearance of jobs and the increase of poverty.
in writing. ‒ the haemorrhaging of skills and jobs in the european steel industry is the result of a slump in demand, which in 2014 was 40 megatonnes below its 2007 levels. i have voted for this report that will equip the european union with flexible and responsive trade protection measures to address the new global industrial scenarios where decisions must be made increasingly swiftly in response to a potential snowballing of inflows of materials, products, information and services.
in writing. ‒ once the backbone of european industry, steel and aluminium plants are now being closed down all over the continent. rising energy prices, stiff and sometimes unfair global competition or excessive regulatory burdens have all contributed to a decrease in the competitiveness of the european base-metals industries in general. the parliament’s report cautions against the risk of a further escalation of this situation in terms of job losses or the indirect negative impacts on high added-value economic sectors such as the automotive industries. it is a problem that needs urgent solutions and as a result this initiative received my full support.
in writing. ‒ i have voted for this report that will pursue the coordination of the carbon emissions allowance, reuse procedures of base metals, forward-looking investments with impact on health and safety, as well as the development of a circular economy, factors that are absolutely vital for europe’s economy.
in writing. the european steel and metal industry is in a difficult situation, due to a significant decline in demand in recent years, which affects both the workforce employed in the sector and other economic sectors such as machine building, building construction and low carbon technologies. the energy and environmental modernisation of these sectors requires an investment policy that few of the companies concerned can currently afford. the creation of the carbon market in 2005 was in line with the eu's strategy to combat climate change, but it created additional burdens for member states' economies. border adjustment can be the solution to avoid the abandonment of the fight against climate change by european sectors at risk of carbon leakage by promoting fair competition between european and non-european producers. this measure can also be applied on a temporary and flexible basis and carbon leakages can be prevented by taking the whole sector into account. border adjustment is the basis of a base metal economy where reducing emissions is linked to investing in reducing those emissions, which are thus profitable. the document before you can be an important step forward.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report on the development of a sustainable european base metals industry, as the european base metals industry is currently facing a significant drop in demand as well as strong global competition, mainly from third countries that do not apply the same high standards and strict regulations as in europe. in this respect, the european base metals industry needs to regain its global competitiveness and a first step in this direction would be the creation of a common energy market, as higher energy prices in europe significantly limit the competitiveness of this industry. in addition, there are numerous sectors that depend on this industry, such as automotive, aeronautics, energy production, construction and packaging. the eu thus needs to improve its competitiveness and maintain its independence in the base metals sector in order not to negatively affect the above-mentioned sectors. in this respect, i believe that the development of new energy-efficient products and new production processes is needed if the eu is to withstand increasingly fierce global competition.

the reporter. commissioner stylianides, i would first like to welcome you and the special representative for human rights, mr stavros lambrinidis, to the debate today on the report on human rights and democracy in the world and the union's policy on the matter. i strongly believe that interinstitutional dialogue is essential to enhance the effectiveness of external action to promote respect for human rights and democratic principles in the union in third countries. in this interinstitutional dialogue, but especially in the communication with citizens, the report that i wrote and negotiated with the other political groups is intended to explain parliament's view on how the european union promoted human rights and democracy in its external relations in 2014. i also took the opportunity to explain parliament's view on the steps the union should take to improve its foreign policy on human rights and democracy. in what follows i shall dwell on a few aspects of the report, a very comprehensive one, with more than thirty pages. one of the key messages of the report is that it is time to focus on implementing the european union's human rights and democracy policy. over the last four years, the union has developed a number of instruments to promote these values, inter alia in response to numerous calls by the european parliament. we now have a very good strategic framework that guides the european union's actions. a second action plan was adopted this year, which translates the strategic framework's priorities into concrete measures. the union regularly organises human rights dialogues with third countries, as well as political dialogues in which rights are addressed. the union has, again as a result of numerous requests by parliament, a very good special representative for human rights. the union has also developed country-specific strategies for promoting human rights, and delegations have set up focal points for the same issues. we have an enlargement policy that promotes rights, as does the recently revised neighbourhood policy. the time has come, i believe, to use all these instruments effectively to maximise their impact on human rights in various third countries. we must have the courage to fully embrace the objective set out in article 21 of the treaty, namely to place the defence of human rights at the heart of the union's external action. i have proposed in this report a number of possible courses of action. among them, i think it is essential to allocate sufficient resources to human rights and democracy policy. the resources can be used, inter alia, to support those who fight every day for the respect of democratic values and rights and principles in third countries. in this respect, i welcome the new support mechanism for human rights defenders working in risky contexts, announced a few days ago by commissioner mimica. a second key message i wanted to convey is that supporting and promoting democracy in external relations must not be a secondary issue in union policy. on the contrary, i believe that respect for democratic principles and human rights go hand in hand and can hardly be thought of separately. i also drew attention to the fact that, in order to truly promote democratic principles, the union cannot limit itself to observing elections in third countries, although this is certainly an important instrument for promoting democracy. in conclusion, i would like to return to the interinstitutional relations we have been talking about, as well as to communication with european citizens. i think it is important that the report that the commission draws up each year takes a more analytical approach and highlights the efforts in this area.

sakharov prize ceremony, an occasion that testifies to the strong commitment of this house to human rights and freedom of expression. as your report states at the outset, mr preda, human rights and democratic freedoms are increasingly under threat in many parts of the world. defending human rights is becoming an ever harder challenge for all of us, in particular, promoting and helping to protect a healthy space for civil society organisations. we are confronted with unprecedented global challenges, with instability and conflicts just beyond our borders, and with a humanitarian crisis even within our borders. terrorist attacks were brought into the centre of our cities, and they are posing an ever—growing challenge to our free and open societies. however, while the years ahead will continue to be challenging for the european union, our approach cannot change. we need more equality and more human rights, not less. to defeat terror, we surely need to improve law enforcement tools. rights. while receiving asylum seekers and migrants, freedom of expression remains the most powerful weapon against radicalisation and terrorism. mr preda, honourable members, your call for placing human rights and democracy at the heart of the eu external relations will not go unheard. the protection of human rights is, and will remain, one of the major priorities of our external action, and it is the foundation that defines all our relations with third countries. this is precisely the rationale of the eu’s second action plan on human rights and democracy, which the council adopted just five months ago. this new action plan shows the common will of the eu, not just of the institutions, but also of the 28 member states together: to continue and enhance their global efforts on defending and promoting human rights and on mainstreaming human rights into all eu policies. this includes development cooperation, migration, counterterrorism and trade. the action plan puts high on the agenda the promotion of gender equality also, women’s empowerment and women’s and girls’ rights. it will serve to measure coherence and coordination between our internal and external policies. overall, it outlines our priorities on human rights in external action and details our strategy for the years to come. the action plan gives a very special focus to empowering local actors and civil society organisations in an increasingly challenging landscape. we need civil society organisations to play an active role in the lives of their countries to the benefit of everyone. during the last years, efforts to bar, restrain, or control the work of civil society organisations have been frequent. restrictive laws have emerged, imposing unjustified and complicated procedures for the registration of associations, or restrictions on their funding, in particular from foreign sources. civil society organisations in our neighbourhood and beyond need our support more than ever. just two weeks ago, we addressed the closing session. she conveyed the relevance that the commission and the eu as a whole attach to the essential cooperation with civil society in the protection and promotion of human rights in the world, and within the european union. this was a first step in a long-term process of cooperation. the eu will continue engaging on this issue. of course, the action plan looks at a number of other priorities. this includes a number of topics that you recall in your report and which we have many times discussed together. for example, we will continue to work on a responsible trade policy, or on promoting the eu agenda on business and human rights. we also want to make social and economic rights increasingly part of our human rights policy. and last but not least, we will use the full range of the policy instruments we have at our disposal. in this context, let me thank you again for the great and extensive contribution of your report. regarding proposals, suggestions and constructive criticism: these are of great value to us. as you suggest, we are working on improving our human rights strategies, making the human rights dialogues and consultations more result-oriented, and assessing the implementation of the guidelines. as regards the annual report, we have already advanced in making it clearer, more analytical and user-friendly from next year. i understand that you are also working on enhancing the ep actions on human rights. i very much welcome, for example, your work on reviewing the guidelines for the ep interparliamentary delegations. it is very welcome. our work does not end, but begins, with the adoption of the action plan. putting it into practice will be a living process where all actors will make their contribution. in that regard, you are, of course, our privileged partners. our actions on human rights and democracy are mutually reinforcing. as just one example, i can mention the role members of parliament play as chief is doing a great job. thank you, stavros. (applause) we all need to join forces and cooperate even further in pursuing the ambitious objectives of our action plan. despite the severe challenges ahead of us, i am sure that we can make further progress, always together.
rapporteur for the opinion of the committee on development.– mr president, above all unity, i think, is very important for all of us. i welcome the final agreement reached on the opinion on the annual report of human rights and democracy in the world 2014. negotiations had been positive and enriching and i believe the opinion will support the work of our colleagues from other committees, especially from the committee on foreign affairs (afet). we made a strong connection between insisting on human rights, gender equality, good governance, peace and security, and the goal of eradicating poverty and inequalities as well as achieving the social development goals in the world. moreover, we recalled that cultural diversity cannot be invoked for infringing human rights which are guaranteed by international law. human rights must be at the core of our development agenda. we therefore stressed the need to ensure that the 2030 agenda for sustainable development is underpinned by the human rights-based approach. we mentioned the importance of the addis ababa action agenda. and we decided to strongly condemn, in the opinion, the use of harmful practices on women and the use of rape as a weapon of war. last but not least, we reminded the commission and member states that agreements concluded with developing countries must include binding clauses on human rights and that the commission must conduct systematic human rights impact assessments of trade and investment agreements. îl felicit pe raportor și pe toți cei care au contribuit la acest raport.
mr president, commissioner, i would like to start by congratulating the rapporteur and by recalling that mrs mogherini has stated that human rights and democracy will be a major priority for her mandate and a landmark in relations between the european union and third countries and civil society. so it created expectations and hopes about that. welcomes the adoption by the council of the 2014 annual report on human rights and democracy in the world and the new action plan for 2015-2019; however, i believe that the council's report should not only contain the results achieved but also the challenges faced by the european union in its efforts to promote democracy in third countries, thus identifying concrete actions that could be implemented in the coming years. events in recent years have demonstrated the need for a new approach, redefining priorities and introducing new working methods, as the one-off policy has not always delivered the expected results and the methods used have not always been the right ones. examples of the failure of this approach are in the states of north africa, where the effect has been devastating, but also in the eastern neighbourhood of the european union. we need to understand that we can be more effective, including from the perspective of measures to support human rights, if we approach this relationship with third countries on the basis of common interests, but at the same time taking into account what differentiates us. we therefore need an integrated approach, covering development, migration, trade policies, supporting third countries in developing administrative capacity for the rule of law, transparent and fair electoral processes and, not least, ensuring access to education, because education is the door through which values such as respect for human rights, tolerance and freedom can enter. education and universal values are the pillars on which modern civilization is built, and where these are lacking, extremism, intolerance and terrorism take their place.

madam president, i congratulate the rapporteur on this fairly balanced report. current legislation provides member states with a set of eight criteria on the basis of which they can decide whether to authorise arms exports. this instrument provides both the flexibility and the rigour needed to avoid the use of weapons against the civilian population or by terrorist organisations and totalitarian regimes. the beneficial effects of the eight criteria contained in the common position of the member states are reflected in france's salutary decision to reverse the export contract for mistral vessels to russia and to stop deliveries. it was a correct decision, motivated by russia's flagrant violations of international law. the arms export control procedure is an important aspect of the european union's foreign and defence policies and therefore needs to be appropriately integrated into the new european union foreign and security policy strategy, especially in view of the current challenges and risks to the security of europe. i would draw attention to the importance of practical cooperation between the member states, europol, eurojust and third countries. this cooperation should be complemented by working procedures on the monitoring of illicit arms trafficking by police forces together with border authorities. the exchange of information and good communication between databases always leads to the reduction and even elimination of these risks. we also need a common and coordinated european union approach to floating arsenals and we need to include in the common position a mechanism for automatically blocking arms export licences to countries against which a european embargo is being imposed.
madam president, the unprecedented spread of armed conflicts is a huge threat to stability and security and has created a less stable and less secure neighbourhood for the eu area. arms transfers to states in conflict are significantly contributing to these conflicts and this unstable situation. i therefore strongly support the report, which will allow a better regulation of arms exports. we have a key role in preventing irresponsible exports of arms to countries that violate human rights and fundamental freedoms, and regulating the international arms trade must be a global ambition. it is fundamental to support transparency and to promote adherence to the highest regional and international standards, such as the arms trade treaty and the eu common position on arms export control. the legally binding framework demonstrates the determination, or at least a first step towards determination, of eu member states to prevent the export of military technology and equipment that might be used for undesirable purposes such as internal repression or international aggression, as happened recently in ukraine, or contribute to regional instability. we therefore have to fully support its implementation in the nearest future.
in writing. i consider this motion for a resolution to be absolutely necessary for the strictest possible control of arms exports. the introduction of eu-wide judicial control of arms exports may be the solution to reduce the loss of life. the way in which this motion for a resolution raises the question of taking into account the export of innovative technologies for licensing purposes and their transfer to the category of dual-use materials and technologies, such as those in the field of robotics and software, is to be appreciated. the speed of technological development in this century means that, in addition to the illegal or illegal export of conventional weapons, robotics or the expansion of software capabilities make available to groups defined as aggressive whole series of civilian applications that can be used as assault weapons. furthermore, these technologies can easily become tools for collecting information to be used for terrorist purposes. in this context, the inclusion of these tools in the list of dual-use technologies in order to control their use much better becomes a necessity. i hope this resolution is just the first step in stopping the delivery of unlawful weapons or dual-use technologies to groups considered aggressive.
vice-president of the commission.– madam president, i am pleased to speak here in parliament today before the vote on concluding the partnership and cooperation agreement between the european union and vietnam, as well as on the protocol for croatia’s accession to the agreement. this agreement will provide a modern and comprehensive framework for the eu-vietnam relationship, which has deepened and broadened over the past few years. twenty-five years ago the then european community and vietnam established diplomatic relations. in these 25 years, our ties have grown from their humanitarian origins to a multifaceted partnership with trade and development at its core. the partnership and cooperation agreement, together with the free trade agreement concluded two weeks ago, will allow us to go even further. today’s debate is an opportunity to acknowledge vietnam’s role as a close partner for the european union in south—east asia and for our relations with asean in particular. as asean’s coordinator for relations with the european union, vietnam has provided valuable support in bringing our two regions closer together. in south—east asia, vietnam is one of the fastest growing economies today. social and economic progress in the last two decades has been impressive as millions have been lifted out of poverty. its foundations were laid in the late 1980s through an ambitious economic reform programme. today, the eu, in turn, is vietnam’s second largest trade partner, the largest development donor and one of vietnam’s largest foreign investors. vietnam is now entering a new phase of national development and aims to become an industrialised country by 2020. to do so it needs to move from a growth model based on low—cost labour to one based on innovation and productivity. this calls for major structural changes and continued investments in infrastructure and human capital. the european union wants a strong and prosperous vietnam, a vietnam that respects the rule of law and human rights. our persistent message to our vietnamese counterparts is that good governance, human rights and the rule of law are the driving force for development, that a free media and a free internet provide huge benefits for vietnam to succeed in the new knowledge-based economy and to meet the myriad of challenges that come with a modernising society, and that greater openness and opportunities for people to participate and actively engage with the institutions are needed to support vietnam’s vision of becoming an inclusive and modern society. it is therefore in vietnam’s best interests to honour its international commitments regarding human rights. let me be clear. the european union and vietnam enjoy a close and ever—expanding partnership but, as in any relationship, there are areas where we have differences. these are, first and foremost, in the critical area of human rights and mrs lochbihler’s report rightly places much emphasis on this. in this respect we noted with concern the arrest today, just one day after the eu-vietnam human rights dialogue, of mr nguyen van dai, a lawyer and human rights activist. we have expressed this clearly to our vietnamese partners. the partnership and cooperation agreement provides us with a much better basis to address issues such as the rule of law and human rights than the framework cooperation agreement of 1996. respect for human rights and democratic principles constitutes an essential element of the partnership and cooperation agreement, with a much broader and more comprehensive set of commitments when compared with the previous instrument. the rule of law features among the fundamental principles covered by article 1 of the agreement. let me assure you that these principles will guide us in our relations. the enhanced human rights dialogue that we agreed to establish in 2012 is the most visible evidence of our commitment here. the latest session was held just yesterday in hanoi. i trust that with the new partnership and cooperation agreement, and thanks to the strong ties between the european parliament and the national assembly of vietnam, we stand a better chance to support vietnam’s transition towards a more open society.

in writing. ‒ economic and monetary union in europe is a concern across all the structures of the european union. while some progress has been made, further efforts are needed to address the current shortcomings of the institutional framework for the euro area. given the significant number of unemployed and those at risk of social exclusion, concrete measures, ambitious and prompt plans are needed to ensure a union based on sustainable development, on equity, ensuring the creation of more jobs, enhanced economic growth and a high level of prosperity for citizens. there is therefore a need to strengthen an economic union that ensures that each economy has the structural characteristics to thrive in monetary union. it is also necessary to strengthen the financial union to ensure the integrity of our currency by limiting risks to financial stability. moreover, the guarantee of bank deposits must be ensured, so that we can speak of a stable banking system as a guarantee of macroeconomic stability. i voted in favour of this report because it requires the adoption of swift measures to strengthen economic and banking governance and the completion of the union's economic and monetary union.
